en: Salutations to Lakṣmī-Hayagrīva, who is the essence of Śrīmat-Dhanvantari, Bhīma, Madhva, Antargata-Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and Vedavyāsa.
This is the *Gītātātparyanirṇaya* (The Determination of the Essential Meaning of the Gītā), composed by the venerable teacher Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
Salutations to the venerable gurus. Hariḥ Oṃ.
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa, who is complete with all auspicious qualities and devoid of all defects, the purport of the Gītā is now being declared.
Among the scriptures, the essence is devotion to the Lord; therein lies the Thousand Names of Viṣṇu and the Kṛṣṇa-Gītā. Through knowledge of these, one is swiftly liberated.
There is no scripture equal to the Bhārata; how could there be one equal to these two?
In ancient times, the Bhārata and all the Vedas were placed upon a scale.
Accompanied by all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, and by all the ṛṣis,
the Bhārata was further expanded there at the very command of Vyāsa.
Because of its greatness and its weightiness, it is called the Mahābhārata;
he who knows its etymology is liberated from all sins.
Nārāyaṇa himself, having been requested by the gods headed by Brahmā, Rudra, and Indra, attained the state of Vyāsa and established the definitive determination of the absolute truth.
He composed the fifth Veda, known by the name Mahābhārata.
Thus it is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*.

Therein, Lord Nārāyaṇa instructs Arjuna—His own dearest, a Kṣatriya of the highest qualification who is a direct incarnation of Indra—who, out of affection for his kinsmen, suspected that the supreme duty of Kṣatriyas, namely the destruction of those associated with Naraka, was unrighteousness and had consequently almost desisted from it. The Lord makes him understand that the worship of the Blessed One through devotion according to one's prescribed vocation is the supreme dharma, and that everything contrary to that is adharma, since all things are dependent upon the Blessed One.
All of this is understood from this very [text].
But if you will not engage in this righteous battle,
then, having abandoned your own duty and fame, you shall incur sin.

By such statements as these, battle is established as one's own duty (*svadharma*). For: "From whom the activity of all beings proceeds, and by whom all this is pervaded—by worshipping Him through one's own action, a human being attains perfection."
Better is one’s own duty, though deficient, than the duty of another well performed. Listen further to my supreme word, which is the most secret of all:
because you are dearly beloved to Me, I shall therefore speak what is for your benefit.
Fix your mind on Me, be devoted to Me, sacrifice to Me, and bow down to Me;
thus you shall come to Me alone—this I promise you as the truth, for you are dear to Me.
Renouncing all duties, take refuge in Me alone;
I shall liberate you from all sins—do not grieve.

By such statements as these, it is established that the worship of the Blessed One must be performed solely through one’s own prescribed duty (*svadharma*), and that everything other than this is to be abandoned.
"Neither by the Vedas, nor by austerity, nor by charity,
nor by sacrifice can I be seen in such a manner as you have seen Me."
But by undivided devotion alone, O Arjuna, am I— such as I am—
capable of being known and seen in truth, and entered, O scorcher of foes.

By these and other such statements, [the Lord] establishes that devotion to Viṣṇu alone is the supreme among all means of realization, and that even for the possessor of knowledge— whether that knowledge be indirect or direct— as well as for liberation itself, dependence upon that [devotion] exists:
"O Pāṇḍava, he who performs actions for Me, who regards Me as the supreme goal, who is My devotee, who is free from attachment, and who is without enmity toward any living being— he comes to Me."
By such passages as these, the devotee’s performance of that [divine] action and the abandonment of prohibited action are established.

Furthermore, by such passages as "Therefore, perform action alone, as it was performed by those of old, even more so by those before them," the performance of the Lord's work is also prescribed for the knower.
This form of mine which you have seen is very difficult to behold;
even the gods are constantly longing for a vision of this form.
"Since you are firmly dear to Me, I shall therefore speak what is for your benefit.
Divine prosperity leads to liberation, while demonic prosperity leads to bondage.
Do not grieve, O Pāṇḍava, for you are born with divine fortune."
But the great-souled ones, O Pārtha, having taken refuge in the divine nature, worship me with undistracted minds, knowing me as the source of all beings and the righteous law.

"By the passage beginning with 'He showed to Pārtha His supreme Īśvara-form,' [it is shown] that Arjuna possesses the status of a supreme qualified disciple and is one who has attained immediate realization (aparokṣajñāna). [As stated:
'Neither the hosts of gods nor the great seers know My origin.'"
For I am indeed the source of the gods and the great seers in every respect. He who knows me as unborn and beginningless, the Great Lord of the worlds,
is undeluded among mortals and is liberated from all sins.
Intellect, knowledge, freedom from delusion, forgiveness, truth, self-restraint, and tranquility;
the seven great seers of old—
this is My manifestation and My yoga.
"I am the source of all; from me everything proceeds.
Thinking thus, the wise, endowed with fervent devotion, worship me. Out of compassion for them alone, I destroy the darkness born of ignorance.
I am the deliverer of those from the ocean of death and worldly existence; having known Me—
the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the Great Lord of all worlds,
and the friend of all beings— one attains peace.
I shall declare to you in its entirety this knowledge along with its realization,
by knowing which nothing further remains here to be known.
I am the origin and likewise the dissolution of the entire universe.

There is nothing whatsoever else higher than Me, O Dhanañjaya; all this is strung upon Me like clusters of gems on a thread. But this most secret knowledge I shall declare to you, for you are free from envy.
Knowledge conjoined with realized wisdom— that by knowing which you shall be liberated from evil—
is the royal science, the royal secret. By me, whose form is unmanifest, all this world is pervaded.
All beings abide in Me, yet I do not abide in them; I am the sustainer of beings, but I do not dwell within beings.
There is none equal to you; how then could there be anyone superior?
Furthermore, I shall declare again the supreme knowledge among all forms of knowledge: My womb is the Great Brahman; in that I place the seed, from that the birth of all beings occurs, O Bhārata.
For I am the foundation of Brahman, of the immortal and the imperishable, of the eternal dharma, and of absolute bliss.
There are these two persons in the world: the perishable and the imperishable.
All beings are called the perishable (kṣara); the immutable (kūṭastha) is called the imperishable (akṣara).
But there is another, the Supreme Person, who is declared to be the Supreme Self;
the imperishable Lord who, having entered the three worlds, sustains them.
Since I have transcended the perishable and am superior even to the imperishable,
therefore I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
O Bhārata, he who, being thus undeluded, knows Me as the Supreme Person, he, knowing all, worships Me with his whole being.
Thus has this most secret teaching been declared by me, O sinless one;
by understanding this, one becomes wise and has accomplished all that is to be done, O Bhārata.
O Pārtha, there is nothing whatsoever to be done in the three worlds;
there is nothing unattained that remains to be attained.

By these and other statements, [it is shown that] there is a distinction between Him and all that is subject to delusion, that everything is dependent upon Him, that He is full of all attributes, that all scriptures have Him as their ultimate purpose, and likewise that liberation comes only through the knowledge of Him, and so forth.
Now, O Viṣṇu, this hymn of praise and sacrifice, worthy of the wise and accompanied by oblations, must be honored by you.
Even while perceiving this Self, one should perform action without hesitation.
When one attains for oneself a well-restrained excellence of bliss.
Pleased by their devotion, the Supreme Lord bestows untroubled knowledge;
and being pleased with them, He grants even greater devotion and reveals His own vision.
One should bestow even greater devotion than that and thereby liberate them from those two;
though liberated, one remains eternally under their influence, endowed with ever-increasing devotion.
Devotion alone is the very nature of the bliss of the goal (sādhya), for there is no other means (sādhana) here.

Having realized that Viṣṇu is superior even to Brahmā, Rudra, Rāmā, and others; that He possesses absolute independence; and that everything is subject to His control—He is the supreme among all therein.
Through Him alone is liberation attained, not by any other means; and vision [of Him] and so forth are the instruments for that realization.
Mortals such as sages and seers are the lowest qualified persons;
the gods are the highest qualified persons; and Prāṇa is the most excellent among them.
Even those who have not attained the state of the gods and are devoid of great vision,
as well as those who are hidden from sight, hear [the sound] either through sport or otherwise.
Through repeated practice of that, even its disappearance shall not occur.
Just as for those sons of Pṛthā, who were instructed by Vyāsa and possessed minds fixed on the Kṣatriya duty, their knowledge became firmly established and remained unobscured.
At the offering of this god Viṣṇu, the subduer of enemies, we approach with oblations;
for Rudra knows his own Rudrian greatness. O Aśvins, you have come upon your radiant path.
In the beginning, there was only Nārāyaṇa; neither Brahmā nor Śaṅkara existed.
Having become a sage, he reflected, and from that these were born:
Viśva, Hiraṇyagarbha, Agni, Yama, Varuṇa, Rudra, and Indra.
There was only one Nārāyaṇa; there was no Brahmā, nor Īśāna. Vāsudeva alone existed in the beginning; there was no Brahmā, nor Īśāna.
Whatever Viṣṇu desires—whether it be Brahmā or Śaṅkara—[he creates].
No one could create Śakra, Sūrya, Yama, or Skanda; there is no creator of this [work].

"It is true that the great purport of all the scriptures is not the supremacy of Viṣṇu, the God of gods; rather, their subordinate orientation toward him is for the sake of the human goal [attained] through everything other than that. Thus says the Paiṅgi Śruti.
"The wise who see the truth will teach you that knowledge," and so forth; this is for the purpose of removing the obscuration of the knowledge already arisen.

They are "prajñāḥ" because they know with excellence (*prakarsena jānanti*). The discourse concerning them is *prajñāvāda*. You speak words contrary to the wisdom and opinion of those [wise ones]. How so? Regarding those whose life-force has departed (*gatāsūn*)... [11]

Indeed, out of affection for your kinsmen, you are causing the abandonment of your own duty. In this regard, is it from fear of the destruction of the body, or from fear of the destruction of the conscious self (*cetana*)? Since the body is in every way perishable, there is no purpose in fearing its destruction. Nor is it from fear of the destruction of the conscious self, precisely because that is imperishable. There is no destruction of me, the Supreme Consciousness; likewise, there is none for you or for these others. As the scripture states: "The eternal among eternals, the consciousness among conscious beings, the One who fulfills the desires of the many. Birth and death are merely the union with and separation from one's own body, as has been explained before.

"For it is only for the individual soul (jīva) that there is liberation from the Lord (Īśvara), but never for Hari [Himself]"—so it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa. Since even the Lord enters into battle, the doubt might arise that He too is subject to both kinds of impermanence due to delusion; therefore, even that is precluded: "But never was I not, nor shall I ever cease to be. Although this doubt did not exist in Arjuna, nevertheless, for the sake of benefiting the world, it is dispelled by the Blessed One. Even while speaking in private, He will manifest that very truth to the world through His form as Vyāsa. 12.

The qualification "of the embodied one" (dehinaḥ) is used to show that even for me there is no attainment of another body. Furthermore, you should not grieve thinking that this will happen to you and others, because we see the body undergoing change even now. || 13 ||
He says that the causes such as not seeing [the Lord] must be endured: "The contacts of the senses," meaning the connections with sense objects. 14.

He states the result: "yaṃ hi" (for whom). Immortality does not consist merely in the absence of suffering; rather, it pertains to the *puruṣa*. For it is stated [in the scriptures]: "Because of the abundance of *brahman*-attributes, one who knows that is remembered as *puruṣa*"; thus, the meaning is that he is called *puruṣa* because he has gone to (*saraṇāt*) the *puru* (the Supreme). || 15 ||

Nor is there grief on account of the suffering in the next world resulting from battle. For it is certain that non-existence does not arise from an evil deed, and existence does not arise from a virtuous deed. According to the *Śabdanirṇaya*: "All words expressing existence (*sadbhāva*) denote happiness; all words expressing non-existence (*abhāva*) denote suffering. Furthermore, as will be stated: "'Sat' is employed in the sense of existence and in the sense of goodness; likewise, O Pārtha, the word 'sat' is used for a praiseworthy action. Thus, because of this certainty, there is no cause for sorrow.

"Only when one knows that 'the non-existent becomes existent,' does one become [existent]"; and so forth. "Anta" means final determination. Nor is this verse intended to negate the production and destruction of what is non-existent and what is existent, because that would contradict direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Everyone in the world conventionally treats the very nature of an object—which is currently designated as "existent"—as being non-existent prior to its production and after its destruction; and there is no evidence whatsoever for the opposite view.

However, this statement is established otherwise: "In the beginning and at the end, it is certain that every effect is non-existent. If that which is non-existent has no distinction here, what is it that is born? For this [argument] is the same even regarding manifestation; otherwise, there would be an infinite regress. Thus it should be understood regarding destruction as well; therefore, the effect is born from the non-existent. Nevertheless, because of the constant experience of non-difference between cause and effect, and because difference is not perceived, the body went to the state of earth. Since such a conventional usage occurs, the experience is always as if it were real. (Brahmatarka)

Furthermore, there is no evidence whatsoever for the claim that nothing exists which is distinct from both the existent and the non-existent. Nor can it be argued that the object of error is something distinct from both because the non-existent cannot appear and the existent cannot be sublated; for one who asserts that "the non-existent cannot appear" must state whether or not the appearance of the non-existent occurred. If it did not occur, then there is no refutation of its appearance. If it did occur, then likewise [there is no proof]. Moreover, there is no evidence that the non-existent appears as non-existent in error, nor that there is no appearance at all. Furthermore, this would entail the undesirable consequence of the total cessation of the conventional usage of the term "non-existent."

Because that form which is non-existent is indeed an error (*bhrānti*) precisely due to its being perceived as existing. Even in the position of indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*), there can be no erroneous status without the perception of existence for that which does not exist—namely, the thought "this silver exists. Even if one accepts the existence of the error itself, it is precisely because of the perception of existence for that which does not exist—namely, "this silver exists"—that one acts toward it as if it were real. Therefore, there is nothing distinct from both [existence and non-existence]. [Scriptural support: "The universe is true" (*viśvaṃ satyam*); "Whatever he intended was true" (*yacciketa satyamit*).
And because of such scriptural passages as: "The Seer, the Wise One, the All-pervading, the Self-existent, has ordained the objects according to their true nature for eternal years. || 16 ||

Although the soul also possesses eternity, the word *tu* (but/however) indicates that being indestructible in every respect belongs to Viṣṇu alone: "Impermanence is said to be of four kinds—the loss of the body, the attainment of suffering, incompleteness, and destruction; the absence of these always belongs to Hari."
"But for all others besides those, some indeed meet with destruction. Thus it is said in the Mahāvārāha Purāṇa.
"The expansion [of qualities] is threefold: by way of place, by way of time, and by way of attributes;
that [expansion] belongs entirely to Hari alone, for no others possess perfect, complete attributes. Thus says the Supreme Śruti. (17)

For embodied beings, however, destruction through the loss of the body and so forth certainly exists. Since the definition of that [Supreme Self] alone is given in the words, "By whom all this is pervaded," the individual souls (jīvas) do not possess fullness either spatially or qualitatively. It is established that suffering is incurred precisely through the involuntary loss of the body and such. Therefore, fight for the sake of worshipping Viṣṇu, who is imperishable and immeasurable; for the cessation of suffering and the attainment of happiness are dependent upon His grace, as stated in passages such as: "But those who, having renounced all actions in Me and regarding Me as the Supreme, for them I am the deliverer."

In the case of the living soul (*jīva*), having already stated that it is "eternal," to say again that it is "indestructible" would be a redundancy. Furthermore, because there is a recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of the very same entity previously described as "indestructible" and "by which all this is pervaded," as being now "indestructible and immovable," [the soul is established].

By the qualification "these bodies," it is understood that for the liberated ones (*muktas*) as well, there exists an eternal body consisting of consciousness and bliss (*cidānanda*) which is their essential nature (*svarūpa*). [This is further supported by the description:
"Where neither passion (*rajas*) nor darkness (*tamas*) exist, nor does goodness (*sattva*) mixed with them, and where there is no progression of time..."
Where there is no illusion, much less others who follow it—there dwell those honored by gods and asuras;
dark and fair-complexioned, lotus-eyed, clad in saffron robes, radiant and well-formed;
all four-armed, adorned with necklaces and ornaments of shimmering, choice jewels, and full of splendor.

"He who shines forth on all sides with the radiant rows of celestial chariots belonging to the great-souled ones— chariots possessing the luster of coral, beryl, and lotus stalks, and adorned with shimmering earrings and crowns—
is like the sky filled with banks of lightning-charged clouds accompanied by most excellent, resplendent goddesses. Thus it is said in the *Bhāgavata*.

"All liberated ones, by means of their body of consciousness-bliss (*cidānanda*), enjoy objects of experience according to their desire, both internally and externally, just like Hari"— thus says the Supreme Śruti.
Nor is there identity between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) even in liberation.
"Having taken refuge in this knowledge, they have attained a state of similarity with me;
even at the time of creation they are not born, and at the time of dissolution they do not suffer."
"He who knows [Brahman] hidden in the secret cave, in the highest heaven—he attains all desires together with the wise Brahman.
"Having approached this Self consisting of bliss, moving through these worlds at will and assuming forms at will, he sits singing this Sāman.

"All his friends rejoice in the glory that has come to them, in their friend who conquers in assembly; for he is the remover of their sin, the winner of their father’s wealth, and he is ready to bestow the prize upon them."

"One, having nourished them, sits chanting the nourishment of the *ṛcs*; another sings the *gāyatra* among the *śakvarī* verses; one speaks as a *brahmán* the knowledge of all that has been born; and yet another measures out the proportions of the sacrifice. "Having attained the supreme light, he emerges in his own true form.
"There he moves about, laughing, playing, and rejoicing. Then the knower, having shaken off both merit and demerit, becomes stainless and attains the supreme equality.
The liberated ones, having attained the supreme Viṣṇu and even though they have taken refuge in His body,
abide according to their relative gradations by means of qualities such as bliss and the rest.
Kings, human gandharvas, gods, and even the ancestors;
noble steeds, karma-gods, those who are the very embodiment of reality, and Purandara.
Śiva and Viriñca are each a hundred times greater than the preceding one in this sequence;
even those others who are liberated are a hundred times inferior to the [former] king.
There is no one equal to Brahmā in any way, even in liberation;
from him, Śrī is a thousandfold superior, and beyond her is Hari.
"Even the Supreme is not equal to it because of its infinite multiplicity.
"Friends with eyes and ears have become unequal in their mental speed.
"Where the desires of desire are attained, there make me immortal"—from such statements of difference even after liberation.

Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with such scriptural passages as: "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15); "Verily, when he does not see there, he is indeed seeing, though he does not see" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.23); "For there is no loss of the seer's vision, because of its imperishability; yet there is no second thing, nothing else distinct from him that he might see" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.23); "He who knows the supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.9); "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7); and "I am Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10). If consciousness were to perish, what purpose would liberation serve for us?
"Having been thus addressed, you have caused me to fall into delusion here."
Yājñavalkya said to his beloved: "I do not speak to you out of delusion;
there is no loss of the knowledge of reality, for one's own innate knowledge is never lost."
Furthermore, there would be no destruction of the object of knowledge; how much less, then, could there be the destruction of the Self?
Although the universe is clearly distinct from Viṣṇu by virtue of its own nature, it is [nevertheless] other than Him.
When [the object] exists in such a way— as if distinct due to a lack of independence—
then there occurs the enjoyment of smell and so forth through the power of the knowledge of one's own nature.
At that time, there would be both self-experience and the very knowledge of God,
when one knows nothing else, neither the self nor God.
How could there be any purpose for human effort, and who would strive for its absence?
Therefore, through the knowledge of their own true nature, they are distinct [from the world] and go to the presence of Viṣṇu.
They enjoy all pleasures, and this is liberation, not otherwise;
for Viṣṇu himself does not perceive another as a second entity.
That second body, which consists of manifestation, does not exist;
whatever else there may be, such as Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and so forth, the Lord is distinct from that.
Because Viṣṇu always perceives [the world] as eternally determined by its state of differentiation, and because he perceives it as such, he does not perceive his own identity with that [world].
There is no lack of distinction between this conscious and unconscious [world] on account of that;
for there is indeed no loss of knowledge in the Omniscient Supreme Lord.
All living beings are Brahman; those who have attained liberation are the Supreme Brahman.
Prakṛti is the Supreme Brahman, and the Imperishable (Acyuta) is the Supreme Mahat.
Neither the liberated ones nor primordial nature ever attain that majesty of Viṣṇu;
yet, through knowledge of Him, one attains one's own true state as Brahman.
If he possesses supreme lordship, then how could there be suffering?
If he is a sufferer, how can there be lordship? For it is only one who lacks lordship who partakes in suffering.
How could there be ignorance in the omniscient one? Where could there be delusion without ignorance?
Therefore, the individual soul (jīva) is not God; rather, it is liberated through His grace.
Because he is beyond what is to be abandoned, the Blessed Lord Hari is the immutable "I";
he is Brahmā because he is full of all qualities; and I am "he" (asau) because he is the immeasurable (a-sana).
He who was called "Asināmā" because he sat upon a seat is addressed as "Thou" (tvam) because of his splendor;
indeed, Hari himself, though one, is the object denoted by all verbs of action, all nouns of substance, and all adjectives of quality.
By means of your words, which are appropriate [to the context], and by means of verbs conjoined with them.
Because of the proximity of the word "we" (asmatpada) and its connection with words denoting action,
as well as because of the remoteness of the word "that" (tatpada), He alone is the primary referent of the meaning.
Having mastered all the Vedas, Śvetaketu, due to his preeminence in wisdom and out of egoism, generally thought, "I am not a mere human being."
Whether he be a god or a portion of Keśava, this wisdom of his could not be otherwise;
thus, filled with pride by such a sense of greatness, he approached his father.
Seeing him standing nearby with his conduct unrefined, rigid, and like one ignorant, his father said:
"O son, from where has this rigidity come upon you?"
For the most part, you have not questioned Lord Nārāyaṇa,
by knowing whom the fruit of the knowledge of the unknown would arise for you.
Because of its predominance and its similarity [to the cause], it is clearly dependent upon that;
thus it is understood as "created by that," for the world would otherwise be devoid of fruit.
If this cognition were independent, it would be false knowledge and cause harm;
for just as from the cognition of a single lump of clay, by virtue of its similarity,
that which is made of clay is known to be "clay" even when it is not currently being produced.
Just as [the word] "clay" and so forth are known to be eternal names,
so too is that which is composed of speech known to be non-eternal, even though it is rooted in that [eternal reality].
Thus, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, is the cause;
he is the primary principle and the independent one, and the entire universe has him as its root.
It is the support of liberation, and it always remains dependent upon that;
it is subtle, all-pervading, and complete, and this entire world belongs to it. Therefore, you belong to it, and you do not belong to it in any way whatsoever.
Just as a bird and its string, and various tree juices;
just as rivers and the ocean, and likewise trees and their roots.
Just as seeds and sprouts, just as salt and water,
just as a person and his location, and just as ignorance and knowledge.
Just as a thief and one who is robbed are distinct, so too are you and the other;
they are eternally different by their very nature, and there is never any unity between these two.
Thus, there is a distinction between everything and the independent Supreme Lord;
how could that which is dependent attain identity with the independent?
That Blessed One, named Jīva because he is the cause of the maintenance of life,
is metaphorically designated as "Jīva" in the transmigrating soul.

All this is dependent upon Him; that Lord is not dependent on anything else. There is the distinction between the individual soul and the Lord, as well as the distinction between the insentient and the Lord; likewise, there is the mutual distinction among individual souls, and the distinction between the insentient and the individual soul.
The fivefold diversity consists of the difference between the insentient and itself, as well as mutual difference;
this is eternal and not something produced, for if it were produced, it would also perish.
Therefore, this fivefold manifold of differentiation is indeed beginningless;
for duality is measured by Viṣṇu’s wisdom and is not imagined through delusion.
This Lord Viṣṇu, the imperishable, is non-dual in the ultimate sense;
he possesses supremacy, absolute independence, and indeed omnipotence.
Omniscience, supreme bliss, and the fact that everything is dependent upon Him—
these and other such qualities belong to Viṣṇu alone and to no one else in any way.
In the doctrine of supreme non-duality (paramadvaita), [these qualities] are indeed non-existent, whereas the other [qualities] certainly do exist.

For from such scriptural passages as, "If the imagined were negated by anyone, then non-duality would exist; [but] for the wise, it does not exist anywhere," it is understood that there is indeed a different object [than mere absence]. Otherwise, the words "single lump," "name," and "designation" would be rendered meaningless.

Furthermore, on that view, there would not be the cognition of everything through a single cognition; for there is no such conventional usage as "one who knows mother-of-pearl is one who knows silver. Moreover, even though [the text] mentions the example nine times, it speaks only of difference (*bheda*). Therefore, one should simply say, "Thou art not That" (*atattvamasi*). Alternatively, *aitadātmyam* means "related to this Self," or "having Him as its master"; thus, "Thou too art indeed of this very nature (*aitadātmyam*)," or "Thou art not He. Furthermore, the neuter gender (*tat*) here is used for the sake of grammatical consistency with the pronoun.

If one were to first present a non-existent Lord and a creation that is not actually attained as being distinct from the Self, and then subsequently negate them, how could the Śruti not be considered the speech of a madman? Furthermore, even a restatement (*anuvāda*)—such as the statement "that which they say is not tenable"—is never seen to occur without a specific reason for its refutation. Otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*): why could there not be a teaching of difference by means of a restatement of non-difference?

Furthermore, because difference is taught at the conclusion of all branches of the Veda, this alone is logical. [Examples include: "One should not teach it to one who has not lived [as a student] for a year, nor to one who is not a teacher—so say the teachers, the teachers"; "I have surpassed the entire world"; "Those who know Brahman know that he is established in the infinite, highest heaven-world"; "I pay homage to the great Viṣṇu"; "They see [Him] abiding within the self," and so forth.
Moreover, neither God nor His difference from the individual soul is established by perception or other means of valid knowledge.
On your view, however, since even oneness and the like would be false and the essential nature [of the Self] would already be established, the Śruti would be rendered purposeless.

Even for that whose nature has been characterized, there is no distinction from its own nature, because it is stated to be devoid of distinctions. Furthermore, if a false distinction were asserted, the scripture would lack authority; and the falsity of those [distinctions] would itself be merely false. Therefore, their reality must be real.

Even if a distinction is produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), since the adjunct itself is illusory (*mithyā*), the very same fault remains: having first brought about a distinction of adjuncts that was not previously attained, one then negates it. Furthermore, even on the view that the adjuncts are real, since the enjoyer is seen as one despite the distinction of adjuncts such as hands and feet, the same faults apply—namely, that all pleasure and pain residing in every adjunct would be experienced by the single Lord (*īśvara*).

[Objection: This is not the same [as the case of the individual soul], because insentient things lack experience. Therefore, it is established that there is indeed a difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord. || 18 ||
He who perceives him as an independent slayer [is mistaken]; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with such statements as, "You slay those already slain by me.
The phrase "him who" (enam) applies equally to the conscious individual and to the Supreme Self. 19.

He states that there is also a scriptural mantra regarding the eternity of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara): "It is not born, nor does it die" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.18). This Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), being already existent, does not become [something new] even in the form of a connection with a body; for death is established as nothing but the separation from the body, as there is no conventional usage of the term "death" for objects such as jars. The non-destruction of one's essential nature is established by the very principle of *kaimutya* (how much more so). This individual soul (*jīva*) is likewise unborn and eternal; otherwise, there would be a tautology. It is also everlasting (*śāśvata*), never abandoning its essential nature through a lack of independence or similar conditions.
"Having little power, lack of omniscience, dependence, incompleteness, and being dependent for one's livelihood constitute the state of a *jīva*; lordship (*īśatva*) is the opposite of that."
"This essential nature of these two cannot be otherwise in any way;
for this very reason, great people declare them both to be eternal.
Thus it is said in the Mahāviṣṇu Purāṇa. He is called *purāṇa* because he goes to (*aṇati*) the ancient (*purā*). || 20 ||
[He perceives] this Supreme Lord as imperishable—devoid of the destruction of the body and so forth—and eternal by His very nature.
For: "Agency is indeed independence; that belongs to the One alone. Knowing that [agency] to be immutable, how could He Himself become an agent?"
Thus says the supreme scripture; otherwise, there would be a tautology with the words "indestructible" and "eternal. || 21 ||
Since for the living being (*jīva*) as well, birth and death are nothing other than the conjunction with and separation from a body, he says that these are not causes of suffering: "Vāsāṃsi... (22).
He states that even from the perspective of its cause, there is no alteration of the Lord: "They do not cut this," [verse 23].

He states that the qualities such as being indivisible belong equally to the individual soul (*jīva*) as well: "This [soul] is indivisible," and so forth. "Eternal, abiding in the omnipresent, and atomic"—this refers to one who is atomic while abiding in the omnipresent. Viṣṇu is omnipresent; "abiding in Him" means being dependent upon Him.
Because it abides in Him by virtue of its cause, it does not move, and is thus "immovable. It is "eternal" (*sanātana*) because it exists together with *nāda*, which is sound.
"The atomic soul is eternally established in Viṣṇu, who is omnipresent."
Nor is its independence from that [cause] undermined even by an examination of the cause itself.
Because he is the vessel for both prohibitions and injunctions, he is remembered as Sanātana.
Thus it is stated in the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa*. Furthermore, the repetition of "this [Self] is indivisible" and so forth would otherwise be redundant.

That in which this [Self] resides is of an unmanifest and inconceivable nature. When the Supreme Lord is known in this way, He brings about the destruction of all sorrow; therefore, you ought not to grieve, as in the passage beginning, "I am the deliverer of those."

For both [the individual soul and the Supreme Self] are introduced by the words, "Never was I not," and because the term "embodied one" (dehin) is used as a qualification for the individual soul (jīva) in various places—such as "indestructible" (avināśi), "by whom all this is pervaded," "of the imperishable and immeasurable," "it does not die," "having been, it will not cease to be," "indestructible," "immutable," and "unmanifest, unthinkable, and unchangeable"—these refer to the Supreme Self as well.

For it is not the case that "all this is pervaded by the individual soul" (jīva); nor is this [Self] primarily an object of cognition. Furthermore, its "indestructibility" (avināśitva) is not something distinct from its eternality (nityatva), as expressed in the phrase "indestructible and eternal. Nor are "unmanifestness" (avyaktatva) and "unchangeability" (avikāryatva) primary attributes [of the individual soul]. Moreover, the statement "having come to be, it will not cease to be" does not imply the non-arising of the body; rather, such qualifications as "indestructible indeed" apply to the Supreme Self, for even the separation from a body does not exist for Him.

Since he is of such a nature, therefore he alone is independent, and everything else is dependent upon him. Consequently, he alone is the bestower of all human goals. Therefore, his worship is indeed a virtuous deed. For this reason, fight for his sake. As for others, however, their bodies are finite, and they are possessors of material bodies (*prākṛtadehin*). Thus, being dependent, they lack the capacity to kill; and because of his eternity, he is not killed. Therefore, those two who think "I am the slayer" or "he is slain" do not understand.

Since this Supreme Lord does not die even in the form of separation from the body, nor is He ever born in the form of union with a body like an individual soul (jīva), He alone, by virtue of His independence, is the slayer of all. As for the individual soul, it is simply this: when the body is slain by Him, the soul itself is not slain. Therefore, how can one who knows the Supreme Self—the agent of all—by reason of such qualities as indestructibility and independence, cause to kill or kill?

Just as one observes the lack of independence regarding the aging of a garment, so too must the lack of independence of the individual soul (jīva) regarding the aging of its own body be understood. However, because the Lord’s body is subject neither to cutting nor other such injuries, He possesses independence.

The statement "they do not cut him" directly demonstrates the absence of cutting and the like for His own body; this is expressed in the present tense. As for cutting and so forth, the Lord displays them falsely only for the sake of delusion. 24.

If the Supreme Self is all-pervading, why is He not perceived as such? To this, He says: "He is unmanifest. How is this possible? Because His power is inconceivable; and that power never becomes otherwise, because He is changeless. To show that all His forms are likewise of this nature, there is the separate use of the words "Him" (*enam*) and "this" (*ayam*). However, in the case of the individual soul (*jīva*), it is for the sake of showing its pervasion through all souls. All of this is established by the Śruti: "He has a true body, the fragrance of bliss, the luster of knowledge, and true prowess."
"He who is knowledge of knowledge, the bliss of bliss, that Viṣṇu is the supreme imperishable. Thus says the Paiṅgi Śruti. "The Supreme Lord is said to be both bodiless and possessed of a body;
because his body is non-material (aprākṛta), he is called 'bodiless'."
This body, consisting of the head, feet, arms, and so forth, is Hari himself;
there is no body other than him, and therefore he is called "bodiless" (adeha).
Since this [Self] is said to possess a body because it is distinct from its own essential nature,
therefore [the body], consisting of the head, feet, arms, and so forth, takes on the form of pleasure, cognition, and the like.
And he is not other than Viṣṇu, because He possesses inconceivable power;
therefore, for Him, there is no connection with or separation from a body in any way whatsoever.
"The Blessed One is heard of as being both of the nature of qualities and the enjoyer of qualities;
for the self-experience of 'I' is experienced by all.
Even though [the Self] is undivided, this distinction is always within the range of experience."
For even a distinction is not other than this [nature], and it is logically applicable to itself as well;
therefore, there is no infinite regress anywhere, owing to the supreme sovereignty of Hari.
Indeed, even what is considered right or wrong is held to be dependent upon Him.
"For when [the nature of the deity] is understood through valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa), how indeed could there be any inconsistency?"—such is the supreme Śruti.
"The qualities heard [in scripture] may appear mutually contradictory in the Lord;
yet even those not heard here should not be a cause for doubt."
"Likewise, faults are both conceivable and inconceivable; for they are not perceived as such by the ignorant. And so forth, in the *Ṛgveda*, in the *Sauparṇa* recension:
"That is one only, without a second; there is no diversity whatsoever here."
"He who perceives here [in this world] as if there were multiplicity goes from death to death.
"Just as water rained upon a mountain peak flows away in different directions,
so one who perceives dharmas as separate runs after those very same dharmas."
Whoever perceives anywhere a distinction among the qualities such as the Fish, Tortoise, and others, or among their activities, or likewise among their limbs;
He who perceives both difference and non-difference goes indeed to darkness;
therefore, a person desiring to prosper should perceive only their non-difference.

Even though there is no difference [between them], a distinction exists; from that, linguistic usage arises—namely, between the qualifiers and the qualified, as well as between the distinction and the thing distinguished.
But this very thing is the distinction; therefore, there is no infinite regress anywhere, whether in the forms of manifestation and so forth, or in the fundamental forms in every respect.
There is never any difference in their capacity, even regarding their qualities:
Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Nṛsiṃha, Vaṭu, Bhārgava, Rāghava, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, Kalki, Vyāsa, and Aitareyaka.
Datta, Dhanvantari, Yajña, Kapila, Haṃsa, Tāpasa, Śiṃśumāra, Hayāsya, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, and Dharmaja.
Nārāyaṇa, and others such as these, are Nārāyaṇa himself in person;
likewise Brahmā and Rudra, Śeṣa and Viṣṇu, Indra and the other gods, and Nārada.
Sanatkumāra, Kāma, Bhava, Aniruddha, Vināyaka, the weapons beginning with Sudarśana, and the universal monarchs (cakravartins) beginning with Pṛthu.
Thus, those such as Lakṣmaṇa and others, as well as Bala and the rest— these three— are distinct from Viṣṇu, yet they are possessed by Hari and are subject to worldly existence (saṃsārin).
Likewise, the re-entry [of the Lord] into Nara, Arjuna, and others is described;
however, O Lord, the re-entry of the Master into the sons of Dharma and others was slight.

"He who knows this has an exceeding love for Hari; but for those ignorant ones who cause confusion [regarding this], their fall into darkness is certain. Thus it is stated in the Mahāvārāha Purāṇa. 25.

Let this elaboration stand aside for now. Even if you consider the birth and death of the living being to occur spontaneously rather than as a fixed rule until liberation, even with that much knowledge alone, you ought not to grieve.

For it is said in the *Śabdanirṇaya*: "The term 'eternal' (*nitya*) is declared to mean both 'everlasting' (*sanātana*) and 'fixed' (*niyata*). In this context, however, it means "fixed," because of the declaration: "For one who is born, [death] is certain. (2.27)
Therefore, one should not entertain the thought that this is something wonderful. || 27 ||

Rather, he says that the Blessed One alone is indeed marvelous: "As if a marvel. He perceives this one, who is truly a marvel, as being like a marvel; he does not, however, perceive him as something non-marvelous. This is like [the expressions] "the sky has the form of the sky" or "the ocean is comparable to the ocean," and so forth.
"The Blessed Lord Viṣṇu is marvelous, because nothing like him exists anywhere;
therefore, knowledge whose object is he is likewise like his own object."
Thus it is said in the Brahmatarka. The qualification "some" is used because even asuras and others perceive [the Lord] as if He were not a wonder. || 29 ||

Why is the embodied soul (dehī) indestructible? Because this Lord exists as the protector within the subtle and gross bodies of every living being; for that very reason, He is indestructible. No one possesses independent power.
As it is said in the *Bhāgavata*: "Substance, action, time, nature, and even the individual soul exist by His grace and do not exist when He is indifferent."

"Stationed here and there, Viṣṇu protects eternally at all times; he is the eternal among the non-eternal, and from that very place he is both eternal and non-eternal. For he alone is the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), the regulator of existence and non-existence. Thus it is said in the Padma Purāṇa. || 30 ||
Having conquered both heaven and earth, according to the Vedic revelation: "Those heroes who fight in great battles... (37).

Sāṅkhya is knowledge that consists of correct discernment (*samyak-khyāti*). Yoga is the means to that [knowledge], defined as "that by which one is joined. As it is said: "Sāṅkhya is the vision of reality; Yoga is remembered as its instrument. Furthermore, the *Brahmatarka* is the treatise on reasoning (*tarka-śāstra*) which was proclaimed by Viṣṇu.
And Akṣapāda, Kaṇāda, the Sāṅkhya, the Yoga, and the logicians (haituka).
The Buddhists, Pāśupatas, and others are proclaimed as heretics (pāṣaṇḍas).
Mīmāṃsā is said to be threefold: Brāhmī, Daivī, and Kārmikī.

"A wise person should study the *Brahmatarka* and Mīmāṃsā for the attainment of knowledge; he should not practice anything else that contradicts Vedic knowledge. Because of this prohibition of other forms of Sāṅkhya and Yoga, [the reference here] is to the Nārada school of Sāṅkhya. This is because that Sāṅkhya is atheistic (*nirīśvara*), whereas the Lord (*īśvara*) has been mentioned [in this text]; furthermore, the followers of Sāṅkhya and Yoga admit that even prescribed violence is a cause of misfortune. However, since fighting is enjoined here for the sake of liberation itself—as in the words, "you shall cast off the bondage of action"—there is no contradiction with the supreme Sāṅkhya and Yoga, as they share the same intended meaning. (39)
"In the Viṣṇudharma, even a mere beginning or a mere desire is not fruitless;

nor does one who performs the dharma of Viṣṇu incur fault by performing another dharma," so it is said in the Āgneya Purāṇa. "Nowhere is there worship of Viṣṇu apart from the dharma appropriate to oneself."
That in which there is neither non-activity nor activity—that indeed is the Vaiṣṇava Dharma.
The gods and other sattvic beings abide in this Dharma;
this is the Kṛtayuga Dharma, the Pāñcarātra, and the Vedic path.
For the sake of pleasing Him, one should never give even a drop of water or a grain of rice to anyone else;
moreover, a devotee of Keśava should always remain free from desire.
One should never entertain even a doubt regarding this, whether it be equal or superior;
one who knows the reality should always understand that everything is dependent upon it.
Furthermore, according to the sequence of the gods who know their respective gradations,
this [devotee] is especially the foremost among those belonging to the primary streams and so forth.
This dharma bestows exceedingly great fruit, especially in the Kali age;
indeed, he who is thus devoted to the Lord is liberated.
Furthermore, another dharma is the worship of various deities according to the three Vedas;
even in that, Viṣṇu is to be known as superior to all in his qualities.
A man who follows the dharma of the three Vedas offers sacrifices and other rites, ultimately dedicating them to Viṣṇu; having enjoyed heaven, he returns again.
One should perform it again and again, going to heaven as long as one remains under the control of Hari;
having fully understood all the gods, one's conduct should always be directed toward that [divine] action alone.
Because of the lack of thorough knowledge of true reality, because of the performance of other [non-salvific] actions,
because of the longing for heaven and so forth, and because of the non-elimination of passion and the like.
Due to the constant failure to remember Viṣṇu, the master of the three Vedas does not attain the Supreme;
however, by gradually surrendering his actions at the end to Viṣṇu, he is liberated.
If one does not know the supreme Viṣṇu despite performing the rites of the three Vedas through many auspicious births according to the rules, [he remains ignorant].
He is not called one who possesses the threefold knowledge; rather, he is called a proponent of the Vedas.
"Vāda" is declared to mean dispute, and "vāda" also means speech itself.
Whether through debate regarding the majesty of Viṣṇu as declared in the Vedas, or even from reciting it,
or from reciting it meaninglessly, one is called a proponent of the Veda.
One should not be devoted to the mere recitation of the Vedas, nor be a heretic, nor a rationalist;
for from them one goes to a terrible, blinding darkness from which there is no emergence.
The Asuras and others enter that path which is described in the Vedas as being without beginning, infinite, eternally miserable, and devoid of happiness.

"The intellect of those who have ascertained the truth is single and devoted solely to Viṣṇu; however, the intellects of those lacking resolve are indeed many-branched and infinite," so it is said in the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa. (41)

Whose intellect is devoid of resolve? The intellect of those who lack wisdom and whose consciousness is carried away by the speech they utter does not abide in composure through its nature of resolve. "Knowledge that accords with the reality of an object is said to be 'equal' (sama) due to that correspondence; however, knowledge otherwise is 'unequal' (viṣama), while composure is a state of equilibrium."
That does not happen to those whose minds have been made turbulent by false words;
for the speech of the mindless is like a flower or music in heaven.
They do not consider liberation to be the fruit,
nor do they regard Viṣṇu— the Lord of the universe— as the bestower of that fruit, which consists of proximity to Viṣṇu.
For the sake of pursuing enjoyments and power, it is a continuous stream of manifold activities that yields the fruits of many cycles of existence and causes one to fall into darkness at the end.
"How could those whose intellects are deluded by that which the evil-minded—who dispute the words of the Vedas—proclaim, ever possess knowledge of reality? And:
"The deluded, regarding sacrifices and works of public utility as the highest, do not know any other higher good."
"Having experienced [the fruits of their deeds] on the back of the firmament, they enter this world or one even lower. Thus says the Śruti of the Atharva-veda.
And in the Bhāgavata it is said: "One should not be devoted to the mere verbal disputations of the Vedas, nor be a heretic, nor a rationalist."
"Those who, due to doubt, do not know that Viṣṇu according to his true nature,
yet are intensely desirous of knowledge, full of faith, and truly virtuous— "
Due to the absence of those who can judge [the truth], being devoid of pure knowledge,
those performers of sacrifices go to the state of humanity once the enjoyment of their heavenly merit has been exhausted.

Those by whom the supremacy of Viṣṇu has been ascertained generally do not go to hell, even through such acts as the killing of a Brahmin; nor do they remain there for long, even when such acts predominate.
However, for those who perform sacrifices and other rites correctly under the guidance of Bhāgavata teachers, there is indeed excellence; for others, however, it is the opposite.
They were outward-looking and did not turn back from their improper conduct,
yet they were [protected] by the splendor of the preceptors who had been gratified with sacrificial fees.
"From that, they quickly go to heaven and then fall into blinding darkness;
others, however, who have their faces turned away from Viṣṇu, do not go to heaven at all.
Thus it is stated in the Nāradīya Purāṇa (verses 42–44).

They are called "those whose domain is the three qualities" (*traiguṇyaviṣayāḥ*) because they cause the poison known as the three qualities to pass away—that is, they cause it to depart. As it is said: "But by relying on the Vedas, they cause [the poison] to pass away—they cause it to depart—thus they are 'removers of the poison of the three qualities' (*traiguṇyaviṣahāriṇaḥ*).
One should always be free from the three qualities, taking refuge in Vāsudeva alone."

"Sattva" [is used] because Viṣṇu possesses the qualities of the virtuous; "ātman" because He is the cause of one's lineage; and "paramātman" because He is my Lord—this is what constitutes self-possession (*ātmavattva*). By means of that, the knowledge of oneness is to be excluded, for one is free from the desire for incompatible welfare and security; otherwise, even the mere act of rising [from sleep] would be impossible. || 45 ||
Due to the overflow [of beings], the absence of any other drinker, and because he is the soul of all,
the Lord Hari, the Sovereign, remains as this well even during the dissolution of the universe.
"For primordial nature (prakṛti) stands enveloping everything in the form of the belly;
therefore, they call dissolution (laya) a state where water has overflowed everywhere.
And: "As long as there is a purpose for the seeker from the presence of Viṣṇu..."
One who knows all the Vedas should indeed be the first to know the Dharma, liberation, and so forth.

"And because the determination of the meaning of the Vedas is proclaimed to be the knowledge of Viṣṇu, and because Hari, being pleased by that knowledge, is the bestower of all fruits. Thus it is said.

The meaning is as follows: even when all waters have overflowed (*samplutodaka*), that Viṣṇu who is *udrikta* (surpassing), devoid of a protector (*pālakavarjita*), and not subject to time and so forth—from Him alone comes the fruit, and that fruit belongs only to one who possesses specific knowledge (*viśeṣajña*) among all the Vedas. For all others than Viṣṇu are not *udrikta* at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*). And those who are *udrikta*—namely the liberated souls (*mukta*) and Lakṣmī (*ramā*)—are likewise not "devoid of a protector," because they are protected by Viṣṇu. Nor are the liberated ones subject to the eightfold afflictions such as time; nor do they possess that same kind of *udrikta*-ness [as Viṣṇu]. Therefore, the well (*udapāna*) is Viṣṇu alone, especially during the dissolution.

"That One breathed, windless, by its own inherent power (*svadhayā*); other than that, indeed, nothing whatsoever existed beyond it. In the beginning, there was darkness hidden by darkness; all this was an indistinguishable ocean. From such scriptural passages as, "In the beginning, this was indeed water, a mere ocean," and "In the ocean, he becomes the one seer, non-dual," [it is established]. || 46 ||

The sense is: "Living beings such as yourself are merely those entitled to perform actions, whereas the fruit [of action] depends upon me. Do not become a seeker of the fruits of action; do not harbor the thought, "I am the Lord. The Paiṅgi Śruti states: "It is He alone who joins this [individual] with the fruits of auspicious and inauspicious actions, yet He Himself does not become joined [with them]. Because He joins him with the fruits of actions while remaining unjoined Himself, therefore that Blessed One is to be known as truly distinct [from the individual]. (47)
Attachment is craving for the fruit. ||48||
"Even when enlightenment has arisen, seek refuge in Viṣṇu alone:
'Hari is the refuge of the ignorant, the wise, and the liberated alike;
those who, due to the predominance of their qualities, consider him to be distinct from all others as if he were identical with themselves [are mistaken]."
Those miserable ones fall into blinding darkness without a doubt;
for those who suffer from perpetual and extreme misery, there is no emergence anywhere.
This applies even to those who know the distinctions between the qualities (*guṇa*) of Viṣṇu, and those who know both His difference and non-difference [from Him].
Likewise, in the case of bodily actions and so forth, or even in the matter of manifestation and the like.
"And those who also revile his own exalted devotees—for all of these, this is the destination; of this there is no doubt," so it is stated in the Nāradīya Purāṇa. (49)
Knowing Viṣṇu as he truly is and performing actions for His sake—this very skill in action is yoga; knowledge of the Blessed Lord alone is wisdom. || 50 || 51 ||

When the delusion of the intellect— characterized by erroneous knowledge— is no longer present, one attains supreme detachment and the fruitfulness of what is yet to be heard and what has already been heard.
Having entered the path of scripture and being steadfast in the knowledge of its meaning,
she is indeed immovable through meditative concentration and because of the direct realization of the Supreme.
"In Viṣṇu he shall attain that yoga; having become liberated, he experiences it. Thus it is said. These two [verses] are specifically established. 52–53.
What is the language? How is it spoken? By what qualities? [It is spoken] by one established in meditative concentration, free from uneven intellect. || 54 ||
"For one who knows, the cessation of all desires can never occur;
rather, it is precisely the absence of forbidden desire that is called 'desirelessness'."
Even for one who possesses direct vision, there may be times when direct vision is absent;
likewise, even one whose desires are contradictory may fight, as Hara fought Hari.
Therefore, as long as there is no overcoming [of the senses], it is described as "vision";
likewise, even the vision that occurs only occasionally belongs to one whose wisdom is established.
If she were indeed fit for liberation by means of the observances alone,
then devotion born of her would not lead to liberation through that sequence.
And thus: "In Viṣṇu, who is the Self"; "by Viṣṇu, who is the Self"; "satisfied solely by His grace. || 55 ||
Passion is attachment. ||59||

Due to delusion—that is, false knowledge—even that which has been known is remembered otherwise; because of this misremembering of the meanings of sentences, even well-ascertained knowledge perishes. (63)
Peace, O Blessed One, is the ultimate goal; for it is said in the Bhāgavata Purāṇa: "Peace is my final state. || 66 ||
When those other than the gods perceive Brahman, nothing else is seen;
it is as clearly manifest as [the sun] at night, such that Brahman cannot be led away by others.
Just as one who beholds a wondrous object does not see anything else clearly, so too [the yogi] does not see other things due to one-pointedness, the abundance of bliss, or like the gods and the sun.
"For generally all [beings] are knowers of everything, and even there, each subsequent one [is more so]," as stated in the *Brahmatarka*.
"For he who, even while enjoying desires, never transgresses the boundary..."
Like the ocean, he who is full of desire is not liberated from that which consists of the Dharma.
The word *ka* signifies that which is contemptible; it is indeed contemptible pride (*māna*).
Desire (*kāma*) is that which is opposed to liberation (*mokṣa*), not every form of longing. Furthermore, life does not persist in the absence of all desire.
"For peace, the vital point, and liberation are found here, since devotion to Viṣṇu becomes firm. Thus [it is said]. (70)
By the mere absence of desire for what is forbidden, one should abandon all objects of sense.
For it is said: "The very notion that what is not one's true nature is one's true nature is indeed egoism (ahaṅkṛti).
Having realized that everything is under the sway of destruction, one must renounce the sense of 'mine' (mamatā) in all things. (71)

*Brāhmī* refers to that which has Brahman as its object. Even for the wise, at the time of death, there may be another birth due to the persistence of *prārabdha-karma* (commenced karma) in those whose minds are otherwise occupied. However, at the moment when *prārabdha-karma* is destroyed, remembrance of the Lord occurs by necessity, and from that, liberation follows. For it will be said [in the Gītā]: "Whatever state of being one remembers when leaving the body... (*Bāṇam*) means the body. As it is said: "Because of the absence of the inert body, Viṣṇu is called *nirvāṇa*;
or because of the non-existence of a separate body, even though he possesses a thousand heads."
And thus [it is said]. ||72||
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā-Tātparya-Nirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānanda Tīrtha Bhagavatpāda. || 2 ||
Hari Om. Knowledge and Yoga have been declared; therein, the Lord elaborates upon Karma-yoga specifically with this chapter.
The seed for the inquiry is provided by the statement: "For action is far inferior... (3.8). 1-2.

Yoga characterized by an abundance of knowledge is *jñānayoga*; the other is characterized by an abundance of action (*karman*). "The Sāṅkhyas, as well as the gods and ascetics, are primarily devoted to knowledge;
among them, the gods are the principal Sāṅkhyas because their knowledge is great."
Although these [others] perform many actions, they experience even more suffering;
therefore, they should be known as the primary Sāṅkhyas, while others are merely yogins of action.
Even for the man of knowledge, there is an abundance of karma; therefore, there are those who practice the yoga of action.
Without both of these, no person whatsoever can partake in the goals of human life.
Indeed, no one ever remains even for a moment without performing action.
"And without knowledge, action cannot accomplish the goal of man.
*Niṣṭhā* means finality or liberation.
"Even so, for the knower, there is the certainty of liberation through auspicious action."

"There is an increase of bliss through one [means] and a decrease through another; however, knowledge [is attained] through action"—according to this supreme scripture (*parama-śruti*), there is no contradiction with such passages as "Not by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth.

Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the complementary portions (*vākyaśeṣa*) of both [texts], such as "Not by the non-commencement of actions," and so forth. Furthermore, equality is established by the passage beginning with "For no one... The statement "There is no other path" also declares that there is no liberation without knowledge. || 3 || 4 ||
"Agency is said to be twofold: modification and independence.

Modification belongs to Prakṛti alone, while independence belongs to Viṣṇu alone," according to the Paiṅgi Śruti. Thus, in the passage "for he is made to act helplessly," the word "helplessly" (avaśaḥ) means "under the control of Viṣṇu," based on such Śrutis as "A is Brahman," and so forth. (5–8)
He states that even such passages as "a living being is bound by action" refer specifically to the actions of those who are not Vaiṣṇavas: "yajñārthāt... (from verse 11).
"The Blessed One Viṣṇu is indeed named Jña; that which goes toward Him is this 'uddeśa' (designation). He who stands firm in the prescribed ritual act is declared to be 'yajña' (sacrifice).
From the production of crops and other such things, the succession of clouds is called 'parjanya'."
He [obtained it] from the sacrifice of R̥cīka, and he too [obtained] all ritual action from Keśava.
Although it is eternal, it is indeed understood from sentences composed of a series of syllables;
sentences are uttered by living beings, they [the beings] arise from food, and that [food] arises from the clouds.
Therefore, Viṣṇu is omnipresent and eternally established in sacrifice. He who does not follow this wheel thus set in motion is a sinner; by destroying the universe, he certainly sinks into hell.

For renunciants, however, sacrifice is primarily verbal and mental; for one dwelling in the forest, sacrifice is without ritual; and for the householder, the entire range of rituals beginning with the *kratu* constitutes sacrifice.
The sacrifice consisting of service and the like is ordained for the religious student (brahmacārin);
the giving of knowledge, fearlessness, and so forth is approved for all as well.

"In the case of a householder, the gift of wealth; for one dwelling in the forest, food and so forth; by all, severe austerity must be performed—thus all are performers of the three duties," so it is stated in the *Nāradīya*.

If there were a reversal of the meaning of the words *brahman* and *akṣara*, there would be a contradiction with the *Pratyabhijñā* [scripture] stating "therefore Brahman is omnipresent," as well as the impossibility of entering the *cakra*. (14) (15) (16)

Although the words *tṛpti* (satisfaction) and *saṃtoṣa* (contentment) are synonyms, there is a distinction between "satisfied by the Supreme Self" (*paramātmanā tṛptaḥ*) and "satisfied in the Supreme Self" (*paramātmani tṛptaḥ*). As stated in the Āgneya Purāṇa: "Through the grace of Viṣṇu he possesses delight; through the grace of Viṣṇu he is satisfied; and being exceedingly satisfied in Viṣṇu alone, he is liberated and beyond the reach of ritual injunctions."

"Rati is designated as bliss (ānanda), while tṛpti is the state of having accomplished one's purpose; prīti, however, is twofold affection—both born of action and innate. Thus it is stated in the *Śabdanirṇaya*. "Santoṣa, tṛpti, āpūrti, and prīti are synonymous terms. Thus it is stated in the *Abhidhāna*. (17, 18)

Because one who is not liberated certainly has duty to perform, therefore one should be unattached. Because by performing action while unattached, one attains the Supreme—this is the meaning of the particle *eva* (indeed), which indicates that duty exists only for the unliberated; this is understood from the word *tu* (but) in the phrase "But he who... Furthermore, otherwise there would be a contradiction with the concluding statement: "Therefore, perform action. [As it is said: "The steadfastness in Brahman, delighting in Brahman, and being fully satisfied by the knowledge of Brahman—there is indeed only a slight difference between those liberated ones and the Pāṇḍavas."

Furthermore, because of this statement from the Bhaviṣyat Parvan, Arjuna does not possess primary eligibility. By the word "alone" (*eva*) in the phrase "he should be one who delights only in the Self," the distinction of the liberated ones from these [others] is shown; for among these [others], there may occasionally arise even the appearance of suffering. (19)
"Janaka and others attained perfection together with action; even those established in knowledge [performed it], therefore one should perform the duty appropriate to one's caste and stage of life.
And: "Action bestows knowledge upon the ignorant, and for the sake of maintaining the world, it is for the wise."
Indeed, she alone grants me satisfaction; she bestows the fullness of the bliss of liberation.

"In me alone there is no need for anything whatsoever; nevertheless, I perform actions for the protection of the world. Therefore, one should act with me as the supreme goal. Thus it is said in the *Kṛṣṇasaṃhitā*.
"Whether by protecting, or by creating, or by withdrawing [the world], [I act] never for my own sake."
Although he is the purpose of Viṣṇu, he nevertheless performs all actions by his very nature.

"Just as one who is intoxicated might perform dancing and other such acts due to a particular state of pleasure, so too does Viṣṇu act because he consists of supreme bliss. Thus says the Barka Śruti. (22–26)
"I am not the doer; Hari is the doer, as is the entire act of worship.
Nevertheless, worship performed by me occurs through His grace and not otherwise."
Devotion to Him, the fruit thereof, His grace again and again,
and the renunciation of all actions unto Hara alone— this is always what brings satisfaction to Viṣṇu.
Because independent agency belongs to Viṣṇu alone and to no other,
his independence is indeed dependent [on others], but only in relation to those who are subordinate to him.
"The modification of the individual soul (jīva) called agency is dependent upon the insentient [matter].

This is to be understood through the sequence: 'The person is the milker, the cow is the milker, and the udder is the milker,'" according to the statement of the *Brahmatarka*. Thus, the agency and non-agency of the Lord, the individual soul, primordial matter (prakṛti), and so forth, must be understood everywhere through their respective distinctions.

"In some places it is *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature), in some places *prakṛti* (primordial matter), and in some places it consists of the three *guṇas*; because he is the supreme agent, the Lord Hari is *prakṛti*.
By their own nature, living beings are of three kinds: superior, inferior, and middling."
Among them, those beginning with the gods are superior; those who are middling are mediocre.
The lower beings, such as the asuras and others, do not undergo any change of nature;
even when there is a transformation of their bodies alone, they return again to their own species.

The highest are fit for liberation; the middling are fit for the path of transmigration; others are fit for the blinding darkness. Attainment [of these states] results from the completion of their respective means.
Due to the absence of fulfillment for all, transmigratory existence is said to be beginningless;
and by the will of the eternal Kālaharī, there is no fulfillment for anyone at all.
Therefore, this beginningless cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra) continues eternally.

Consequently, for the lowest living beings, all [defects] such as false knowledge (mithyājñāna) and so forth should be known as their natural qualities; among the intermediate mortals, these are found in a mixed state.

Knowledge of reality, devotion to Viṣṇu, and so forth— by these [qualities] directed toward the deities and others, every person, being powerless, is indeed made to perform action; for it is by Viṣṇu alone that these natural qualities are made the cause [of such activity].
While actions are being performed, the one of deluded intellect thinks, "I am the doer"; however, the knower of reality knows that those qualities such as desire and the rest belong to Viṣṇu.
However, regarding the soul's innate desires and so forth, they always exist as the motivators; my independence [over them] is never present.
Thinking thus, one should not be attached; for the Lord is pleased with him who is deluded by the qualities of his own nature regarding that which is superior in qualities such as knowledge.
They claim that the Self alone is the agent by its own independence;
they do not know that those qualities, as well as that action, are dependent upon Viṣṇu. A knower of reality should not reveal the truth to those who are unworthy of it.
One should speak in the form of debate, never in the form of instruction;
or one may speak in the form of a courtier when questioned, or indeed remain unmanifest.
"For even having understood this, since he always acts in accordance with his own nature, all beings follow their own nature; what will restraint accomplish?
Thus it is stated in the *Prakāśasaṃhitā*. (35)
He asks about the impeller that exists prior to the Supreme Lord and the gods: "Now, by what? (3.1.1) [36]
Viṣṇu is the impeller of all, while Brahmā and others are his subordinates;
the Asuras, however, are the presiding deities of lust and other passions, directing them solely toward inauspicious ends.
There, Kāma, who has Kālanemi as his charioteer, stands enveloping all people— those of good, middling, and inferior character— in succession, like smoke that rises and spreads.
"This [desire] is not enough for that great eater; therefore it is called *anala*, like fire.

One who eats while possessed by the senses is consumed by the very weapon of knowledge (*jñānāstra*). Thus it is said in the *Brahmatarka*. Furthermore, it says: "Knowledge is 'covered' (*āvṛta*) because this [desire] covers it in the form of an obscuration of knowledge. Not only is it difficult to fill, but it is also considered to be insatiable; thus it is *anala*.
"And even for fire, desire is 'non-fire' (analas), insofar as one considers it 'not sufficient' (nālam). Thus [ends the section] 37–41.
"The gods, beginning with Indra, who consist of the senses, are superior to all; Rudra, however, is the presiding deity of the mind over them, and Sarasvatī is superior even to him."
From that, Brahmā, the Great Self (Mahātmā), is remembered as the excellent one whose nature is intellect;
Lakṣmī is the excellent one whose form is unmanifest; and from her, Hari himself is the most excellent.
"There is none equal to it, nor indeed superior"—thus has the sequence been proclaimed;
by awakening to this order, the enemies such as desire and the rest are to be destroyed.
"And the supreme station of Viṣṇu, which is incomparable, is attained swiftly.

Nor is there any contradiction with such statements as, "The objects are indeed superior to the senses," or "Rudra has the form of the ego (ahaṅkāra)," for all the gods who possess self-conceit [are arranged] higher and higher.
Their separate status is proclaimed solely in order to express their superiority.
In this matter, the intended purport of the scripture is held to be precisely the sequence of superiority;
for while those in higher stations exist, the others do not exist in the lower ones.
"Nevertheless, whatever belongs to the father is also attributed to the son;
for all entities, beginning with the unmanifest, have their respective presiding deities.
And from such scriptural passages as: "Whatever belongs to the son belongs to the father, and whatever belongs to the father belongs to the son; this is what is meant by that. And so forth.

"In the case of words that denote many things, the determination of their specific meaning is understood through gender, context, and so forth, as well as from the predominance of the cause for their application. Thus it is stated in the *Śabdanirṇaya*.
"Where there is equality of gender and other such factors, it is indeed the frequency of usage [that determines the meaning]."
"In that case, he would be the decisive authority; therefore, one should be very well-versed in the scriptures. Thus it is stated in the Brahmatarka. (42) (43)
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavadgītā-tātparya-nirṇaya* composed by the venerable Ācārya Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda. || 3 ||
Hari Om. This chapter consists of a detailed expansion upon both knowledge and action that have been previously mentioned:
"That knowledge consisting of the Pañcarātra, which was formerly given by Viṣṇu to Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, and Sūrya, Vyāsa imparted to the Pāṇḍavas."
It is declared that among those very descents, He bestowed the Gītā in brief upon Arjuna in the midst of the army when he was desirous of fighting.
Just as the deities perform their actions and just as they know them,
so too do all those of the Kṛta Yuga and the kings beginning with Manu.
And that which is to be known and that which is to be performed by all seekers of liberation born in the three ages beginning with Tretā has been declared therein in the Gītā.
The Pāṇḍavas and others, who desire security, will act [accordingly] and understand it;
likewise, there is no scripture anywhere equal to that Gītā.
"The Pañcarātra is to be known as that which fulfills the meaning of the Vedas in its entirety;
this Gītā is its summary. Therefore, there is nothing equal to it anywhere. Thus it is stated in the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa. 1.3.
"Even though they already know, virtuous men ask for the sake of knowing the specific details or for the sake of firm conviction;
therefore, O Pārtha, you ask. From this statement in the *Āgneya Purāṇa*, it follows that Arjuna does not not know the Blessed Lord. (4–5)

"By his own *māyā* means by his own will. 'Presiding over his own *prakṛti*' means over his own nature; for there is the scriptural authority [of Śruti] stating, 'This is the nature of the Divine,' and so forth. For this very reason, the word 'own' (*sva*) is used as a qualifier in passages such as 'presiding over his own *prakṛti*. However, in passages such as 'by me, the supervisor, *prakṛti* [is set in motion],' the word 'own' is not used. In passages such as 'know my supreme *prakṛti*,' another [nature] is understood because it is perceived as being related [to the Lord]. But here, the word 'own' denotes his essential nature (*svarūpa*)."

Regarding the term *svabhāva*: here too, one's own (*sva*) nature (*bhāva*) is *svabhāva*. The word *bhāva* is used, however, to eliminate the suspicion that it might refer to a relational entity (*sambandhin*). Furthermore, the expression *svasvabhāva* serves to eliminate the suspicion that it is merely a metaphorical usage (like the expression *svarūpa*, "own-form").

"The imperishable Viṣṇu, having as his inherent nature the state of being a creator and so forth, performs creation and other acts by his own will, and he himself becomes manifold. Thus says the Nārāyaṇa-śruti. (6) (7) (8)
"Those qualities whose knowledge is said to lead to liberation individually in the Vedas and the Itihāsas— liberation, however, results from their collective integration."

"In this very way [liberation comes] from tranquility and the rest, and not otherwise by any means whatsoever," according to the statement in the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa*; thus, in passages such as "birth and action" (*janma karma ca*), liberation does not result from that alone. (9)
"And: 'Those by whom the preeminence of Hari is considered to be the primary [principle]—O Blessed One, they should be known as being absorbed in Me (mayi-mayāḥ); they are liberated, and no others.
Thus it is said. *Madbhāvaḥ* means devotion (*bhāva*) toward Me. || 10 ||

In that very same way, I worship [them] by bestowing fruits that follow from them. Even for those who sacrifice to other deities, a perfect result arises only through dedication to Me and by following the path of Viṣṇu. As stated in the Āgneya Purāṇa: "Even the worship of another deity, when finally dedicated to Him, shall become the cause of results such as heaven; otherwise, one should not worship Hari. (11-12)
