And: "The four castes are divided by the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas; indeed, those who possess sattva alone are Vaiṣṇavas. Furthermore, he will describe the distribution of duties with the words beginning "tranquility, self-restraint," and so forth.

"Vaiṣṇavas are indeed *sāttvika*, while others are *tāmasa*; their distinction based on caste and so forth arises from the difficulty or ease of attainment. And: "The natural status of being a Brāhmaṇa and so forth is distinguished solely by qualities such as tranquility (*śama*)."
The distinction created by the different types of yogis is to be understood as merely adventitious.
"Devotion to Viṣṇu follows [the Lord] among all castes; yet, starting from the Lord of the worlds, it diminishes, and thus the distinction is innate. So it is said in the Nāradīya Purāṇa.
Furthermore: "The Lord Viṣṇu, though the agent, is also called the non-agent."
"And because there is no other creator of that [universe], owing to the independence of the Supreme Self.

Furthermore, the word "api" (also/even) serves to include the qualities; it means: "Know also that I have no other creator. The qualification "me" is used to exclude identity with the individual soul (jīva). (13–16)
It should be understood that even our karma arises from me, and so forth. || 17 ||

Regarding action (*karman*) and the individual soul (*jīva*): because of its lack of independence, the soul is "non-action" (*akarman*). Because of the absence of both ritual injunctions and fruits, Viṣṇu is "non-action" (*akarman*); yet, due to his independence, he is the agent of all actions.
"It is called 'action' (*karman*) because the soul (*jīva*) is measured (*mīyate*) within it;
because he is immeasurable (*amita*) by means of the word 'injunction' (*vidhi*), the Lord Hari is 'non-action' (*akarman*)."

Thus it is stated in the Nāradīya [Purāṇa]. The word *kara* ends in the letter *ra* and denotes the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), or it denotes action (*kriyā*), because [the soul] is dependent upon that. Furthermore, the term *karman* (action) is well-known in the Pañcarātra as referring to the individual soul (*jīva*), because it performs all actions and because it yields the entire fruit [of those actions]. || 18 ||
The Blessed One is without dependence because he is the very basis [of all]; for one who is liberated, there is the conceit of independence. (19–23)

How is there the abandonment of the sense of agency? [The text says: "Offering to Brahman," and so forth. Offering to Brahman is *brahmārpaṇam*. The oblation is Brahman; the fire is Brahman; the ritual action is Brahman—along with the meditative absorption (*samādhi*). The meaning is that even meditative absorption is dependent upon That.
As it is said in the *Mahābhārata*: "The Lord alone is independent; everything else belonging to Him is said to be dependent. (24)

They worship Viṣṇu alone as the divine sacrifice; because He is their own object of enjoyment, He Himself is the sacrifice. They offer the sacrifice of action into the fire called Brahman by means of that very Viṣṇu who is known as the sacrifice. || 25 ||
They practice restraint of the ears and other senses as a form of worship to That; they enjoy sense objects as a form of worship to That. || 26 ||
They practice restraint of the senses as a form of worship for Him. The phrase "by sacrifice alone" is to be connected with every instance.
As it is said: "One should worship Him by that [sacrifice] alone, or by other prescribed means;
that indeed shall be the sacrifice to Viṣṇu, whether mental or accompanied by external rites."
Thus, in the Brahmavaivarta [Purāṇa], verses 27–31.

In passages such as "the ears and so forth," since no object of sacrifice (ijya) is mentioned, one might suspect that the object of sacrifice is something other [than the Self]. He dispels this doubt by stating, "spread out at the mouth of Brahman.
And [it is said]: "The supreme Brahman, known as Viṣṇu, the imperishable, is to be worshipped with all sacrifices. || 32 ||

All action in its entirety, from every side—even the slightest—is brought to completion within knowledge; when knowledge arises, it is fulfilled. In the phrase, "Those seven whom you consider the best in archery, who have completed their learning," the word *samāpti* (completion) here signifies fulfillment (*pūrti*). This is because of the subsequent mention of yoga: "Having cut this doubt of yours with the sword of knowledge, take recourse to yoga. (33)
Because He will say later, "I shall declare to you that knowledge along with realized wisdom," He Himself will indeed teach it. || 34 ||
In me, who am all-pervading; therefore, precisely because of that pervasiveness. (35–40)
One who possesses self-control and is devoted to the Supreme Self. || 41-42 ||
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavadgītā-tātparya-nirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda. || 4 ||

Hari Oṃ. With this chapter, [the Lord] clarifies the characteristics of yoga and renunciation (saṃnyāsa). Having raised the doubt that in such passages as "one who has renounced actions through yoga" (yogasaṃnyastakarmāṇam), the word *nyāsa* refers to the abandonment of all actions, he asks about renunciation (saṃnyāsa) with the intention of showing that yoga and renunciation reside in different types of persons. || 1 ||

These two are suitable for a single person; the intention of the reply is that between the two, yoga alone is superior. Both are to be combined, because it will be stated later: "But renunciation, O mighty-armed one, is difficult to attain without yoga. || 2 ||

The meaning of the word *saṃnyāsa* is simply the avoidance of hatred and so forth; it is not intended here as the stage of life (*āśrama*) of the ascetic (*yati*). Thus he says, "is to be known. Nor is there any contradiction with the statement, "the renunciation (*nyāsa*) of actions performed for desire," because that too constitutes a form of renunciation when combined with this. Nor is there a contradiction due to the separate mention of "renunciation" (*tyāga*), because *tyāga* is a specific sub-division of *nyāsa*, just as the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas are distinct groups within the same lineage. || 3 ||

The ignorant, however, by the term *nyāsa* (renunciation), accept only the stage of life of the ascetic (*yati-āśrama*), and believe that the qualification for the knowledge denoted by the word *sāṅkhya* belongs only to those in that stage, while the qualification for the action denoted by the word *yoga* belongs only to householders. The wise do not hold this view. Why? Because one who is properly established in either the path of knowledge or the path of action attains the fruit of both. Therefore, even action must be performed by the knowers of truth, and even for householders who perform action, the Lord must be known;
for without knowledge, the proper performance of action does not occur.
Action performed without desire and preceded by knowledge is called "withdrawn" (nivṛtta) here;
by practicing that which is withdrawn, one attains the eternal Brahman.
Without causing injury, the ascetic should worship with flowers or with the *praṇava*,
or with the root mantra, [realizing] Brahman whose essence is Vāsudeva.
Even for one who possesses the vision of Brahman— the certainty that "all things end in liberation"—
there shall be an increase in bliss while performing the rites of Viṣṇu.
Action devoid of the vision of Brahman is proclaimed not to be primary;
therefore, they say that action is that which is performed by one who perceives Brahman.
For even householders go to the world of those who have renounced because of this;
therefore, there is indeed no distinction between the path of knowledge and the path of action.
"Therefore, this distinction of stages of life (āśrama) arises from the contraction of [worldly] action," according to the Vyāsa-smṛti. || 4 || 5 ||

"In the *Āgneya-purāṇa* it is said: 'Yoga is the means to liberation; indeed, renunciation (*nyāsa*) itself takes that form. When performed as an offering to Viṣṇu, it is auspicious; renunciation is never otherwise. Without the nature of yoga—such as being offered to Viṣṇu—the mere abandonment of action results only in hell, because it will be stated later: 'O Pāṇḍava, know that which they call renunciation to be yoga. Renunciation is mentioned separately because it is a specific type of yoga. (6)
"The primary yoga is that of one whose self has become the self of all beings.
And it is said: "Because he takes up all beings, Viṣṇu is proclaimed as the Self;
therein the person whose mind is fixed on the Being is one whose self has become the self of all beings. (7)
He explains how renunciation (nyāsa) takes the form of yoga with the words beginning with "not at all anything," and further:
"The knower of reality indeed knows that the mind and other faculties, impelled by Viṣṇu toward their objects in every way, function [thus], and that there is no other independent agent. (8–9)

The dedication to Brahman consists in thinking: "These acts of worship performed by me are for my own spiritual welfare. The non-agency of the individual soul (*jīva*) is due precisely to its lack of independence.

As it is said: "Just as one's own salutation may be caused by a father yet performed by the child, so too, although the worship is performed by the individual soul, it remains dependent upon Viṣṇu. (10-12)
Therefore, renunciation of action is by means of the mind alone, with respect to the lack of independence [of the agent]. || 13 ||

Just as the status of being a protector granted by a father belongs only to princes, so too there might be the suspicion that the agency characterized by independence in actions, as well as the independence regarding the results of those actions—such as merit (dharma) produced by them—which are granted by the Supreme Self, also belong to individual souls (jīvas). He dispels this doubt with the words "not agency," and so forth. The meaning is that the Lord does not create for the world independence in action, nor in the production of unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), nor in the fruit [of action]. Otherwise, the qualification "for the world" would be redundant.

Just as a king does not give away his subjects to his own sons—despite those who live in the realm and subsist on their wealth—because he retains sovereign authority over them, so too it is logical that the Lord does not create [the world] for those who are joined with the fruits of karma and the like, because He retains His sovereignty over them. The Blessed One is *svabhāva* (Self-nature), meaning He exists and causes things to exist by Himself. Because He is *svabhāva*, He engages in agency and other functions entirely of His own accord.
As it is said: "The Blessed Viṣṇu is celebrated as *svabhāva* due to His sovereignty;
this sovereignty of His is never surrendered to another at any time."
"Even for one who acts, there is no connection with sin and the like solely due to [the Lord's] sovereignty;
because their intellect is shrouded by ignorance, they do not recognize Him as such."

Thus, in the *Mahāvārāha*: "I am the source of all," "I heat [the sun] and I send down rain," "His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold, consisting of innate knowledge, strength, and action," "Nothing whatsoever is done without You," "This is the very nature of the Divine," and "But as in the world, His activity is mere sport"—from such passages, His agency is not non-innate, nor is He merely an agent. Furthermore, this is because there is an absence of any contrary evidence, and because this position is already refuted by the rejection of the theory of indeterminacy (*anirvācya*).

Furthermore, for those who maintain that [Brahman] is devoid of all specific qualities (*viśeṣa*), there is no distinction whatsoever from the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*). For when it is said that something is "devoid of all specific qualities," it does not thereby follow that it exists; this is because even properties such as being denotable (*vācyatva*), being definable (*lakṣyatva*), and existence (*astitva*) are themselves specific qualities. Otherwise, words such as "Brahman exists" would suffer from the defect of being synonyms. Moreover, a specific exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is necessarily based upon a specific thing to be excluded (*vyāvartya*); otherwise, it would be utterly meaningless. Furthermore, that which is undenotable by any word cannot be the object of a definition (*lakṣya*).

Furthermore, there is no proof whatsoever for the claim that nothing exists which is beyond the scope of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Non-existence, however, is established through non-perception, just like a seventh taste and so forth. And so-called "self-luminosity" (*svaprakāśatva*) is not established by any means of knowledge. If self-luminosity were something distinct [from the object], then one would have to accept a specific attribute (*viśeṣa*). If it is not distinct, then that very thing falls within the scope of a means of knowledge. In the absence of any means of knowledge, if one merely negates being illuminated by another, then because there is no proof for self-luminosity, the result would simply be non-illumination.

"Establishment by implication" (*arthataḥ siddhiḥ*) means establishment through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), or establishment by that means of valid cognition (*tat-pramāṇa*). In either case, there would necessarily be the status of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*). Since the term "self-luminous" (*svaprakāśa*) does not admit its own being-measured (*svamitatva*), nor does it admit being measured by another (*paramitatva*), there is simply no proof [of self-luminosity]. Even when "luminous" (*prakāśa*) is stated, it is never observed without something to be illuminated—whether itself or another—just like eating and so forth. Furthermore, the contradiction between the agent and the object is contrary to experience; for knowledge is never observed without the object of knowledge and the knower.
Therefore, there is no distinction whatsoever from the doctrine of emptiness (śūnyavāda). Consequently, because it entails infinite faults, we desist [from further discussion].
"Hari is by nature the agent; everything else is impelled by him.
Therefore, that agency of his never perishes. Thus says the Paiṅgi Śruti. (14–17)
"Viṣṇu is always equal toward all living beings, even those in adverse conditions; for even in one who has fallen to the state of grass and such, the qualities of Hari are eternally complete. (18–20)
If even now one finds happiness merely by remembering the Supreme Self, was he not already perfectly united with Him at that time? || 21-23 ||
He has become Brahman; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the statement that "he goes to Brahman. Furthermore, internal happiness and so forth arise from the vision of Brahman. (24–37)
"One who perceives reality is indeed liberated, even while not yet liberated, because of his resemblance to the liberated.
How much more so one who has actually attained liberation! Therefore, knowledge alone is superior for a human being. Thus it is stated in the Nāradīya [Purāṇa], verses 28–29.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavadgītā-tātparya-nirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda. || 5 ||

Hari Oṃ. Meditation is described here: "The great-souled ascetic established in Brahman indeed offers the bodily fire into his mouth," and so forth; thus, even for the ascetic, there is no absence of fire, because of the superimposition of the Self. || 1 ||
The meaning is that renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is indeed a particular form of yoga. || 2 ||
One who has perfected the means is one established in yoga (*yogārūḍha*).
[It is said: "Service to various people is called 'action' (*karma*);
it should be performed by one seeking yoga (*yogārthin*), but by one established in yoga (*yogastha*), there is abiding in Hari."
By him also, service should be rendered to those superior to himself by others in all matters according to one's ability; this is the distinction between the unaccomplished and the accomplished.
One who has attained the means is a Siddha; one who desires [the goal] is called a Sādhaka.
By his assistance to living beings, the Lord becomes satisfied.

"Therefore, for one who has attained the means (*siddhopāya*), meditation, exposition, worship, and so forth of Viṣṇu must be performed, and nothing else; by that alone Keśava becomes pleased. Since there is such a statement regarding those engaged [in practice], there is no contradiction.
Furthermore, the *Bhāgavata* states: "Tranquility (*śama*) is the fixing of the intellect upon Me; self-restraint (*dama*) is the control of the senses. (3)
How does one not become attached? By renouncing all volitional constructions (*saṅkalpa*). For it has been said: "All actions [are performed] in Me," and also:
"Knowing that this world is dependent on Me, one is called 'My renouncer'. (4)
One should indeed deliver the individual self from the cycle of transmigration by means of the Supreme Self;
for Viṣṇu is the eternal kinsman of the virtuous, yet the enemy of the wicked.
"He who is conquered by devotion born from grace toward Him remains under His control;
he is a friend to that person, but to anyone else he is like an enemy. And:
"The Supreme Self is concentrated," as the remainder of the sentence implies. || 5 || 6 ||
"Knowledge is said to be the cognition of Viṣṇu’s preeminence everywhere; the thorough knowledge of His specific attributes is celebrated as higher knowledge (vijñāna). Thus [it is said]. (7–8)
"Whosoever acts according to the conduct prescribed for them in a particular situation—that is knowledge or equanimity; otherwise, it is inequality. Thus it is said in the Mahāviṣṇu Purāṇa.
Furthermore, one who possesses affection without a motive is a friend who acts for the benefit of others once they have recognized [the need].
An enemy who commits acts such as killing is a *mitra* (friend), whereas one who merely performs disagreeable acts is an *ari* (foe).

"One who is indifferent even toward those who are affectionate, who lacks attachment, and who merely imitates what they do, should be known as a neutral party; among friends, such a person is distinguished. Thus it is stated in the Nāradīya [Purāṇa], 9.19.
The self is Viṣṇu; by the self, that is, by His grace. (20–26)
It has become Brahman. || 27-28 ||
The Supreme Self abiding within all beings. || 29-30 ||
"Viṣṇu alone exists everywhere"—thus it is established. || 31 ||
Therefore, one should show affection toward those who follow Viṣṇu just as one does toward oneself. || 32–36 ||

*Ayati* means "without effort," because of the supplementary statement, "but one who exerts himself through effort. Even though the word *yoga* has the general meaning of "means" (*upāya*), there is no contradiction here, as it is intended to refer specifically to a particular means such as meditation-yoga (*dhyānayoga*) and so forth. (37–43)

"One who merely desires to know the means to liberation is superior even to a mere reciter; how much more so one who knows it, and especially one who is established in it"—thus [it is said] in the *Paramayoga*. (44–45)
"Among austerity, sacrifice, and the like, meditation alone is superior;
knowledge is superior to the meditation of the ignorant, and therefore meditation accompanied by knowledge is the highest."
Even in that regard, for one who lacks devotion to me, meditation on another is not effective;
such a person knows only what is common to others regarding me, and perceives me as being no different from another.
Those who view others as inferior, those who are indifferent, and those who are hostile are non-devotees;
for even my devotee who, for the sake of some purpose, might meditate upon another deity [is not a true devotee].
"Therefore, my pure-minded devotee alone is superior to all others who are dependent on me, for he knows this; he is immortal through his retinue. Thus spoke Dattātreya. (46–47)
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā-Tātparya-Nirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānanda Tīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
Hari Om. The greatness of the Blessed One is now described in detail.
"Among infinite living beings, only some indeed strive for liberation; and among those, it is clear that only some are liberated once others have been liberated."
"Only a few, such as Brahmā, Rudra, and others, know Hari perfectly;
for others, their knowledge regarding Hari is supreme only to the extent that their liberation has been attained. Thus it is said in the *Padma Purāṇa*.
"Even among the liberated and the perfected ones, he who is devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa..."
"One whose self is perfectly tranquil is extremely difficult to find, even among millions, O Mahāmati," so it is said in the *Bhāgavata*.
"All devotees of Hari are liberated, but among them, Brahmā is foremost;
however, one who is the supreme devotee of Viṣṇu is considered superior even to him, being a mass of pure life-force (*jīvaghana*)," so it is stated in the *Sattattva*. (3)
Nature is considered to be of two kinds: insentient and sentient.
Among these, the insentient consists of the three qualities (guṇas), while the sentient is Śrī, the beloved of Hari.
Both of them are subject to Viṣṇu and are considered the causes of the world;
Viṣṇu is the father of the world, while Śrī, who is insentient, is the mother.
"And that very [ignorance], impelled by Viṣṇu's power, is the material cause (upādāna) of the world. Thus [it is said]. 4-6.
The meaning is that there is nothing higher than I, and I alone am the highest; otherwise, the word "anyat" (other) would be redundant. As it is said:
"The individual souls (jīvas) alone are proclaimed as 'lower' due to their connection with suffering;
but Śrī alone is the 'higher' because her nature is eternally free from suffering."
But because it is not afflicted by suffering, the middle wind is so called;
because its nature is not dependent on anything else, and because its bliss is neither unequal nor excessive.
And because everything is dependent upon Him, Viṣṇu is considered supreme;
since there is no other [entity] in between, the suffixes -tara and -tama have the same meaning here.
Because of her fitness for such a relationship, even living beings are considered inferior.
But those who are even lower still, being averse to the consciousness of Hari, are fit only for eternal suffering; for this [consciousness] could not exist in that which is insentient.
He who knows Viṣṇu as even higher than this is liberated;
being liberated, he becomes the Supreme Radiance through the enjoyment of eternal bliss.
Even therein, there is a gradation; among them, Brahmā is considered superior.
The realization of Viṣṇu’s superiority over all is called knowledge.
Having thus distinguished that knowledge, it is proclaimed as "vijñāna" (discerning cognition).
And this exists in varying degrees among Keśava and the others;
therefore, Viṣṇu is the primary possessor of knowledge, while the others possess only slight knowledge. || 7 ||
Abiding in the waters, he tastes them and is therefore known as Rasanā;
abiding in the sun, moon, and other luminaries, he shines forth and is thus called Prabhā.

Because he, who resides in the Veda and is named Praṇava, praises the Self (ātman), he is therefore [called] Praṇava; because Keśava, residing in the ether (kha), causes all things to sound, he is named Śabda.

Abiding in the earth, he himself perfumes both the meritorious and the non-meritorious; abiding in fire, he bestows brilliance; abiding in the elements, he grants life; and abiding in ascetics, he purifies them through austerity. 9.
From its manifestation it is designated as the "seed";
from its awakening it is named "the Awakened," established among those possessed of intelligence. || 10 ||
But because its power is eternally full, that power is free from desire.
And because he has no army of kings and employs others in their respective positions, his very self consists of such strength; he is himself the bestower of strength upon the strong.
Or rather, it may be called *pūrṇatva* (fullness) because it is the strength of delighting in that [state];
for generally, desired objects tend to destroy virtue, but Hari [protects] them again.
Desire does not cause the destruction of dharma; rather, when desired in accordance with dharma, it causes the increase of dharma.
Therefore, Viṣṇu, whose desire is never opposed to dharma, is established within all beings.
Thus he is distinct from everything else, independent, omnipresent,
and the Lord who, by his very nature, bestows everything upon all at all times.
And those states which are characterized by goodness (sāttvika), as well as those of passion (rājasa) and darkness (tāmasa)—
Therefore, this [world] does not depend on anything other than that, nor does he depend on it.
Not dependent on anything else. || 12 ||

"Yet, because it is measurable by this [intellect], the world is utterly deluded by Viṣṇu through Māyā, who is under his control like Lakṣmī. But those who take refuge in Viṣṇu indeed cross over that Māyā."
Lakṣmī and that goddess Jaḍamāyā—both of them are under the control of Viṣṇu; therefore, with exclusive devotion, one should go to him for refuge.

If the kind of devotion one has toward Him does not exist at all toward anything else, that should be known as exclusive devotion (ananyabhakti); indeed, that devotion must be directed toward Viṣṇu alone.
One may indeed practice devotion toward others—such as Lakṣmī, Brahmā, Hara, and so forth—as being Vaiṣṇavas, but not otherwise; for they are entirely under His control.
In this way one attains the goal, and not otherwise by any means whatsoever;
for the reality is complete in the one Vāsudeva, and there is no other.
Such a person is rare in this world, for all others perform sacrifices by mixing [deities],
failing to recognize Viṣṇu as the Supreme while regarding Ramā, Brahmā, Hara, and the others [as his equals].
Indeed, even while performing sacrifice, one enters into terrible darkness and constant suffering;
however, for one born into a family of the ignorant, as long as there is no worship of Viṣṇu,
and as long as one does not know the reality of Viṣṇu, service [to Him] must be performed separately.

If, having understood this, one performs the worship of another deity anywhere for the sake of worldly enjoyments such as knowledge and the like, one should not do so unless it is for the purpose of becoming an attendant.
What is done unknowingly and then abandoned will not lead to fault;
however, if it is not abandoned, it will surely continue to bring about rebirth and other such states.
"And let the Blessed One himself quickly make known [this],
if he intends to take some [being] from another birth as his own [disciple]," and so forth.

From the concluding statement, "Know them to be from Me alone," and because they possess those respective names due to being the causes of those [effects], it is determined that [the Self] bears those names. Furthermore, because the opening statement, "All this is strung upon Me," is made with a sense of distinction; and because the word *ātman* refers to the knower of truth as one who "attains Viṣṇu," based on such passages as "that which he attains" and "that which he takes"; and because of the complementary passages such as "for he is established [in Me]" and "he resorts to Me. "At the end of many births, one becomes possessed of knowledge; thereafter, he resorts to Me."

Knowing that "Vāsudeva is all" and that He is the Fullness; and because of the perception of difference in the supplementary passage, "Those who worship other deities [attain them]"; and also because of the statement: "The worshippers of the gods go to the gods, but My devotees come to Me as well. (21-22)
Having recognized the supreme nature of Viṣṇu, a person who worships the gods separately goes to those gods;
but failing to recognize that, he falls into darkness itself.
"Nevertheless, as long as they do not ascertain equality, inferiority, or oneness with others, they are born again and again in saṃsāra. Thus [it is said]. 23.
"That Supreme Self is unmanifest, while the individual soul (jīva) is declared to be manifest. He who considers these two to be one goes to the lowest darkness. Thus [it is said]. (24–25)
"Just as Hari knows Himself, others do not know Him at all;
Ramā and the others know Him only slightly and gradually by His grace. Thus it is said. (26)
"Dualistic delusion" (*dvandvamoha*) is false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*).
As it is said in the *Mahābhārata*: "One should know that *tamas* is the darkness of night, and *moha* is indeed perversion.

Here, "duality" (*dvandva*) refers to the individual soul (*jīva*), the Lord (*īśvara*), and so forth. Delusion regarding these objects is "dualistic delusion. "Confusion" (*saṃmoha*) is the persistent clinging to that [delusion].

"Attachment to that [duality] is called great delusion, darkness, and anger," so it has been said. "At the time of creation (sarga), indeed at the very moment of creation, he who perceives the attributes of the individual soul in the Lord, or the attributes of the Lord in the individual souls, or who perceives the identity of the soul and the Lord—he is called one possessed by the delusion of duality," as stated in the Āgneya Purāṇa. (27–29)
Having thus spoken, he removes the suspicion that there might be something else by saying, "together with the elements and the divine. (30)
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-gītā-tātparya-nirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānanda-tīrtha Bhagavat-pāda.

Hari Oṃ. Following the previous explanation, the attainment of Brahman is now described. Because of the qualification "That" (tat), it was stated that "Brahman" refers to something specific among primordial nature (prakṛti) and the rest. However, since the word "and" (ca) in the subsequent phrase "and that which pertains to sacrifice" (sādhiyajñaṃ ca) implies the inclusion of the objective world (adhibhūta) and so forth, there arises a doubt: "Is the knowledge of Viṣṇu something entirely different? This is the reason for the question, "What is that Brahman? Since it is well known that the Supreme Imperishable (paramākṣara) is primarily Viṣṇu himself, he answers accordingly.

The same resolution applies to the objection that even for the ignorant, that [Self] must be made known; for the doubt that the word "I" was not used again is resolved by the fact that the term *avyakta* (the unmanifest), as employed specifically for Viṣṇu in the phrase "the Unmanifest having attained manifestation," refers to the Imperishable (*akṣara*). However, in the passage "those who worship the Imperishable, the Unmanifest," it is determined that this is indeed something else, because there is a separate inquiry, because a gradation of fruits for the two types of worshippers is stated, because it says "the Immutable is called the Imperishable," and because it declares Viṣṇu's superiority in the words "I am even higher than the Imperishable."

The statement "I alone am the Adhiyajña" is made in order to eliminate the sense of duality that might arise from the expression "together with the Adhiyajña. Its being "accompanied" (sahita) is appropriate in view of its other form residing within the bodies of all living beings:
"Viṣṇu, dwelling in the bodies of living beings, is called the Adhiyajña."
That very same [reality], in its all-pervading form, is celebrated as Brahman.
Because he is the object of various superior sacrifices and because he is magnified by them, he abides in the Supreme Self.
The creation of those beings who are insentient by nature is known as the work of Hari.
Because they consist predominantly of the elements (bhūta), living beings are called "pertaining to the elements" (adhibhūta);
Viṣṇu alone is the supreme deity (adhidaivata), and she who belongs to him is Ramā.

"This should be understood by men as being called Puruṣa, Prāṇa, and Adhidaiva," so it is stated in the *Tattvaviveka*. As for the question, "In what form is He the Adhiyajña?", it is answered by the statement "I alone [am He]," and thus the definition is implicitly provided. ||4||

"Madbhāvam" means the state of being in Me; that is, the disposition toward Me. For those who are constantly permeated by that state, they abandon [the body] while remembering [Me]; thus, there is merely remembrance at that time. However, even for one who remembers, just as in the case of a lapse from samādhi, attainment occurs through a memory following the momentum of previous karma. For those with direct realization (aparokṣajñānins), it indeed happens that they remember and abandon [the body] upon the exhaustion of their prārabdha-karma, because it has been said: "And at the time of departure, they know Me. Because of the qualification "yuktacetasaḥ" (of those with disciplined minds), direct realization arises only for those who remember [Me] constantly.
"Through devotion, through knowledge, through the constant abandonment of prohibited acts, through the perpetual remembrance of Hari,
and through the non-abandonment of prescribed duties without attachment— by these very factors combined."
"Direct perception of Viṣṇu arises [only through this], and never otherwise. Thus, in the *Sattattva*. (5.8)
Beyond darkness, he possesses a non-material body. || 9-10 ||
Brahmacarya is the fixing of the mind and other faculties upon Brahman. || 11-12 ||
Because it is denoted by a single syllable, the Supreme Brahman is the "Single Syllable" (ekākṣara). || 13-15 ||
"Nevertheless, the existence [of the soul] following birth belongs only to one who is liberated;
however, for those who have transcended Maharloka, there is no birth without the dissolution of the portions of the body."
"Even there, they will inevitably and quickly regain that very place," thus it is said in the Padma Purāṇa. 16.
"A thousand" means a great many. Of Brahman, the Supreme Brahman:
"At the arrival of day, all manifest forms arise from the unmanifest;
at the arrival of night, they dissolve back into that very thing known as the unmanifest."
This is because of the remainder of the statement (*vākyaśeṣa*). For it is not the case that the dissolution of all individual manifestations occurs at the very end of a day of Viriñca.
And as it is said: "Even for the eternal Hari, this time consisting of two *parārdhas* is metaphorically designated as his 'day' and 'night' due to the cessation of activity. (17–22)

In this context, those who have departed immediately after death [attain the goal] through the presiding deities of time (*kālābhimānidevatā*). Although fire (*agni*), light (*jyotis*), and smoke (*dhūma*) are presiding deities of non-time (*akāla*), they are referred to as "time" because of the predominance of time [in their nature].
As it is said: "The son of Fire is established in two ways—as fire and as light;
having reached him, the one most devoted to Brahman proceeds to the presiding deities of the day and so forth."

Thus, regarding the true nature of reality (*sattattva*): when there is an intention to describe death at that specific time, there is a conjunction with fire, light, and smoke. For it is heard in scripture that even for one who dies during the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*), there is the attainment of Brahman without return, as stated: "Now, he who dies in the south, having gone to the greatness of the ancestors, attains union with and residence in the same world as the moon. These two indeed are the greatnesses of the sun and the moon; the learned Brāhmaṇa conquers them. Therefore, the Brāhmaṇa attains greatness. And in the *Pādma Purāṇa*: "The wise man attains Brahman, regardless of where he may die. (23–26)
"And he who perceives both the path and Brahman directly and without mediation, transcending all merit and remaining undeluded, goes to that supreme Brahman. Thus [it is said]. (27-28)
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-gītā-tātparya-nirṇaya*, composed by the venerable Ācārya Śrīmad Ānanda Tīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
He elaborates upon what was stated in the seventh [verse]. 1-3.

"Even though all beings are situated in Viṣṇu, they do not abide in Him, for He is unattached," so it is said. [The Lord says] "my Self" to remove the doubt that the body might be the Self, since the body is non-conscious; for [the Self] is not different from that [body]. (4.9)
"The term *adhyakṣa* is declared to mean 'lord' (*adhipati*), because the senses (*akṣāṇi*) are under his control," according to the *Śabdanirṇaya*. || 10 ||
"A human-like woman" means one resembling a human being. And it is said: "Though Viṣṇu is non-different from her body, he is dependent upon it because it is under his own control.
Furthermore: "The view of equality regarding Brahmā, Rudra, Rama, and others is 'non-difference';
however, perceiving defects even in those who have appeared as incarnations is 'incompleteness'."
To perceive a distinction in the descent of the Dharma-body and so forth, and to regard the various incarnations as separate, is known as "confusion" regarding Janārdana; it is ignorance.
All the merit of one who disregards Keśava is in vain;
moreover, even though he has attained a manifestation [of the Lord], he goes to the lowest darkness.
"He should be known as having a body consisting solely of consciousness, free from defects, and endowed with perfect, auspicious qualities. Thus it is said in the Bhaviṣyat Parvan, 11.14.
"Whether as a single form, or four forms, or five forms, or divided into twelve and so forth, Hari is worshipped by the virtuous. Thus it is said. (15)
He is the Ṛgveda because he is worthy of worship; he is the Sāman because of his equality even toward those of lowly form;
he is the Yajus because he is the object of sacrifice; he is the Sacrifice because he is omniscient; he is the Puruṣottama because of his supreme nature;
he is the Kratu because his very essence is action; and he is Svadhā because he is sustained by none other than himself.
This mantra protects one from pride; it is a treasure-trove of powers and a medicine for all ailments.

"Because he is superior (*jyāyas*), he is named *ājya*; because he holds the *darbha* grass, he is *darbhara*; because he is invoked (*āhūta*), he is *huta*; and because he is the leader (*netā*) who brings about arrival (*āgati*), he is *agni*. And so forth.
Thus, although Acyuta is distinct from each of those objects, he possesses their respective names in this way.
"Because of His sovereignty, because He is the creator of all, and because of the infinity of His qualities, He is absolute. And:
"Since He is made manifest by the syllable 'Om', the Blessed Lord Hari is the *oṃkāra*.
And: "He protects, therefore He is the Father; He measures, therefore He is the Mother; since He is greater than the Father..."
He is the Grandfather because he bestows [all things], and he is the Repository because he protects those who are afraid.
"And because he is the refuge and the manifestation, the Lord is called the Seed. Thus it is said.

He is *pralaya* because he is the destroyer at the time of dissolution; he is *mṛtyu* (death) because [he acts] even at other times. "Moving within the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the sustainer of the vital breath, dissolving that which is immortal..."
"The dissolution of the universe is called death, which is distinct from the act of killing. And:
"Because He is full of all excellent qualities, there is none other superior to Him in attributes;
therefore, the supreme state known as Viṣṇu is declared to be 'Asat' (the Non-existent). Thus it is stated in the *Śabdanirṇaya*, verses 16–19.
"Because of sacrificing to no other deity, because of the intensity of devotion, because of being free from desire,
and because of constant yoga, he is indeed superior even to the Vaiṣṇava who knows the three Vedas."
For by that alone, all [the gods] beginning with Brahmā would belong to the devotee of the Lord (bhāgavata),
even more so for one who sacrifices to Keśava through horse-sacrifices and other rites.

"Those who are Vaiṣṇavas honor other deities precisely with the understanding [that they are Viṣṇu]," so it is said in the Āgneya-purāṇa. And: "Worship (upāsā) is the act of attending upon [the deity] through the correct knowledge of the multitude of its qualities. (20–23)
Because it has been said that "having worshipped me, they pray," even though they know [Him], they do not recognize Him in His true essence.
As it is said: "He who does not know Keśava as the best of all gods—his merits are in vain, and he certainly goes to blinding darkness."

Furthermore, because it has been stated that "their hopes are vain and their actions are fruitless," the passage beginning with "they fall" does not refer merely to those who lack knowledge, nor to those who possess false knowledge. Therefore, this result accrues even to those who, despite knowing Viṣṇu’s supreme preeminence, fail to recognize that Brahmā and the others are His attendants and so forth. (24–28)
"Even one who is a devotee of His is not [automatically] dear to Him if he is hateful, nor is one who is not a devotee dear if he is beloved;
rather, Hari bestows fruit according to the degree of devotion, and is therefore impartial"—thus it is said in the *Padma Purāṇa*. "Out of affection for me, they [are dear to You]" (29–31).
Even the performance of sinful acts by men is natural;
likewise, virtues such as being a Brahmin and so forth are meritorious and are indeed attained through their own inherent nature.
Even men may fall into womanhood through sin or even through desire;
however, women do not attain manhood, for they are women by their very nature.
By virtue of the boon granted, her residence shall be within the male body together with that man.
In that birth, those excellent women who are born from sinful wombs become her own true wives,
just as the final body is dear to all living beings.

"But upon liberation, one's own true nature shall manifest, even at the conclusion of the experience of karma"—from this statement in the *Bhaviṣyat-parvan*, it follows that the epithet "meritorious" applies to those of sinful birth. (32–33)
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-gītā-tātparya-nirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānanda-tīrtha Bhagavat-pāda.
Hari Oṃ. The phrase "the hosts of gods" and so forth is for the purpose of illustration. 1–2.
The beginning of even that which has no beginning is itself without beginning. || 3 ||
"Because it is a treasury of awakening, that internal organ is called 'buddhi' (intellect)," according to the *Śabdanirṇaya*. (4)
"Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,

and the highly effulgent Vasiṣṭha are remembered as the ancient seven ṛṣis"— thus it is stated in the Brāhma Purāṇa. "The Manus, due to their specific excellence of knowledge, are remembered as the gods, beginning with Brahmā."
According to the distinction of castes such as the Brahmins and others, they are fourfold, though they are many.
Due to their wretchedness, other gods bear names such as Brahmā and others;
a sacrifice performed by non-Vaiṣṇavas is consumed by these wretched deities.
The sacrifice was performed by the Vaiṣṇavas, indeed by the gods known as Manus;
and his sons, Marīci and the others, are remembered by the name Mānavas.
His sons and grandsons were the sages, as well as the Mānavas and Manavas;
from them came human beings—thus this creation arose from Viṣṇu.
Thus, in the Mahāviṣṇu Purāṇa. || 6 ||

"That by which one is joined is yoga; it is both a means (upāya) and power (śakti). And: "Vibhūti is distinguished manifestation; it is either greatness or manifold manifestation. Yoga is capability. (7)
By the phrase "they worship Me," [the author] dispels the doubt that the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) are one. || 8 ||
Their lives are absorbed in me; their activities are directed toward me. (9.20)
Those forms of Viṣṇu, by whose proximity other objects acquire a state of excellence through their own nature, are indeed called *vibhūtis* (manifestations).
The Lord named Brahman, who has entered into Brahman because he is the collection of all deities, is the cause of superiority; abiding in the Sāmans, he is named Sāman.
"In the *Vibhūtitattva*, it is stated: 'The cause of superiority over the Vedas is Hari, who likewise resides in the *aśvattha* tree;

the cause of excellence among trees is he alone who is named *aśvattha*. And because it has been asked, 'In which and which births do these [manifestations] exist?', it follows that the form of the *vibhūti* is indeed distinct from the individual souls (*jīvas*) such as Brahmā and others."
The manifested form (vaibhava-rūpa) is of two kinds: perceptible and concealed.
That which consists of Kapila, Vyāsa, Kṛṣṇa, and others is known as the perceptible manifestation.
"It is distinct from Brahmā and other individual souls as well as from insentient matter;
residing within them, it bestows upon them their respective excellence of species, yet its majesty remains concealed. And so forth.
"The Self is to be known as 'Ravi' (the Sun) because its qualities extend everywhere, just as the sun [pervades all things]."
The Marīci Sāman arises from the movement of the rising clouds, due to its state of equilibrium.

Because he is bliss and the essence of bliss, he is Śaśin; because he is knowledge, he is Veda; because he is sensation, he is Hari; because he dwells in the sky (va), he is Vāsava; and because he is consciousness, he is Cetana.
He is Pavana because he is sought by those who protect [the world], Bodhana because he awakens the mind,
Pāvaka because he purifies, Meru because he is the support of the body, and Sāgara because he is the ocean of the syllable *mā*.
Skanda is so called because of his extraction from the essence; Bhṛgu because of the world’s streaming forth [from him];
Japayajña because of his burning away [of sins]; and likewise Jātapas because he is one who has performed sacrifice.
The Aśvattha tree stands in the form of a horse, and Śrī and Ira take refuge therein.
Because he gives everything that Airāvata gives to men, he is Nārada;
and because he is the refuge of modesty and prosperity, he is called Himālaya.

Vajra is so called because he is to be avoided by his enemies; Vainateya because he is the refuge of those who bow to him; Vāsuki because he bestows residence (vāsa) and happiness (sukha); Kandarpa because he destroys the distinctions of pleasure;
Aryaman because he is the knower of noble mothers (aryamātṛ); and Kāla because he calculates (ākalanāt).
Varuṇa is so called because he wards off; he is a pair, possessing two forms, since he exists both within and without.
He is Makara because he creates pride; he is Yama because he restrains; he is the omnipresent Lord because he governs all.
He is Prahlāda because he is supreme bliss; he is Mṛgendra because he seeks out the Lord of creatures.
Jāhnavī is the one who causes those who abandon their station to attain the supreme state; the Lord of the selves is the inner self;
Vidyā is so called because its nature is pure consciousness; and Hari is the Word because he is the object to be expressed.
Kīrtya is the speaker, Kīrti is the locus, Vāk is the name Śrī, Smaraṇīya is memory, and Smṛti is likewise the form of Meghākṣa. Thus it is proclaimed.
Because it is intent on play, *dyūta* (gambling) protects those who sing;
because it possesses the quality of goodness, *sattva* (purity) protects; and because it punishes, it is called *daṇḍa* (the rod).
He is Bṛhatsāra and the immeasurable; he is Bṛhatsāma and the lord of the Uśanas;
he is the bringer of knowledge of the auspicious and inauspicious, and is proclaimed as Kusumākara.
Knowledge is the silence of the nature of knowledge; he is the sage worthy of praise, and his conduct is the method of leading.
Because he has reached the end of all paths, he is proclaimed as Mārgaśīrṣa.
Kapila and Vyāsa drank [the nectar] with ease and even sportively;
he is named Viṣṇu because of his excellence, due to the supreme bliss of his vital breath.
Thus Viṣṇu, who abides in various living beings and other forms, is celebrated by various names according to his manifold qualities and is designated as "Vibhūti" (the Manifestation).
In certain cases, such as with the hare-mark and others, he is established as the autumnal moon by bestowing lordship over heterogeneous things;
in cases such as Śarva and others, he exists by bestowing preeminence among homogeneous things.

Because Brahmā is superior even to Śakra, Uśanas, Arjuna, and others by virtue of belonging to the same class as a portion of that [divine nature], he is also higher than the gods, being immediately next to Viṣṇu.
Just as there is no one equal to him among those possessing qualities such as poetic skill,
so too is Bhīma among the sons of Pṛthā, and knowledge is supreme among sacrifices.
And among weapons, the Sudarśana is mentioned; among the Vedas, the Ṛgveda is spoken of—thus it is stated in the *Vibhūtitattva*.

In some instances, there is a preeminence of the Sāman, depending on the presiding deities (*abhimānin*): "The Ṛks are Śrī, Gī, Umā, and others; the Sāmans are Prāṇa, Śiva, and so forth"—this is due to the distinction between the presiding deities. In those cases as well, [the assignment] is according to what is appropriate. (21–40)
It becomes joined with a portion of my splendor. || 41 ||

The phrase "What is the use of knowing? serves precisely to indicate that what is about to be described possesses a superior fruit; otherwise, the statement itself would be redundant. As it is said: "In some cases, something auspicious is mentioned for the purpose of indicating the superiority of another;
one should not, however, consider that [the first] to be blameworthy, but rather recognize the excellence of the other."
"And when both are combined, it is even more beautiful than that. Thus [it is said]. || 42 ||
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā-Tātparya-Nirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānanda Tīrtha Bhagavatpāda.

Hari Om. From such specific descriptions of His form as, "the immutable Self, the supreme divine form... the God consisting of all wonders, infinite, with faces on every side," it is established that this form consists of divine majesty and is eternal; from that very fact, its nature as consciousness, bliss, and so forth is also established. Furthermore, because He said, "my body," the distinction [of His form] from the sun and other luminaries is established. And from statements such as, "my forms," "the infinite form on all sides," and "I wish to see Your form," it is established that there is a single, undivided, infinite form.
The single form of Hari, due to His connection with inconceivable sovereignty,
appears as the object of manifold numbers solely by virtue of its specific manifestations.
Wherever the absence of difference is established by valid cognition,
it is precisely there that the so-called "particular" (viśeṣa) exists, being devoid of any further particularization.
The particular (viśeṣa) is its very nature, and it is self-sustaining;
although eternal in its substance-nature, it arises as the very essence of a particular.
The particulars (viśeṣas) are indeed eternal; thus, in this way, it is twofold.
The nature of the entity exists as non-different [from them] in the beginningless [series].
In all things, distinction is known from experience alone;
nothing whatsoever can be expressed, defined, or measured without being qualified by such distinction.

If the qualified entity were distinct from itself by its own nature, it would follow that the self is not an object of cognition; thus, the qualified entity could not be known, and due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it would not exist at all.
For even "by itself" (svayam) is devoid of any specific property of selfhood;
it cannot be known as that which is qualified, and likewise [the qualifier], thus there is an infinite regress.
In the absence of difference, there is no contradiction, since everything is both known and unknown;
that very same thing is known in its form as known, and unknown otherwise.
Furthermore, because that which is undivided is qualified, neither of the two faults applies;
this is due both to the experience of oneness and to the experience of distinction.
And because of the experience of that knowledge, the occurrence of those two defects does not exist;
moreover, difference and non-difference are not qualifiers of the agent and the enjoyer.
Since no one whatsoever has the experience "other than me," there can be no distinction of a qualifier, nor any internal difference, anywhere.
Because in passages such as "of pure nature," non-difference alone is observed;
and because there is a rule of non-distinct perception regarding power, knowledge, and so forth.
The unity of external particulars exists only through the perception of their difference, and not otherwise.
If a threefold division of gods is postulated even in the absence of a specific cause,
then faults such as the excessive burden of conceptual construction (kalpanā-gaurava) are highly applicable therein.
Neither identity nor plurality exists in the insentient by necessity;
for difference and non-difference are experienced there, as they are perceived otherwise.
"I am one" and "another is different"— since difference and non-difference are established in this very way among sentient beings, there is no single uniformity.
Since that which is known as "one" is again known as "many," such as a cloth and so forth, how can there not be both difference and non-difference?
To whom has a cloth directly appeared as something other than its threads?
If it were non-different from them, how could there be an absence of the cloth when the threads exist?
Furthermore, the self (ātman) cannot serve as an example here,
because the pure notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya) demonstrates non-difference in that case.
In this case, there would indeed be an infinite regress due to the distinction of parts;
moreover, no partless entity could ever be within the scope of any means of valid cognition.
Since its parts are perceived through distinctions such as front and back,
even a limiting adjunct (upādhi), being connected to only one part, [makes known] that which is indeed existent.
How could that which swallows all distinctions make them known by dividing them?
Therefore, qualities and so forth do not exist anywhere in an absolute sense.
Even while a real entity exists, there occurs the conventional usage of existence and non-existence;
likewise, difference and non-difference, as well as qualities and so forth, reside in an insentient entity.
The existence of qualities and so forth in consciousness is held to be in the form of potentiality,
based on such common usage as "this sleeping man is strong" or "this learned man [is wise]."
Nor is there ever any empirical usage regarding an insentient thing in the form of its potentiality;
that [reality] is indeed one without a second, and here there is no diversity whatsoever.
He who perceives here [in this world] as if there were multiplicity goes from death to death;
just as water rained upon a mountain peak flows away in different directions.
"Perceiving the dharmas thus as distinct, he follows after them alone"—
from such scriptural authority (*śruti*) and because of His supreme sovereignty,
everything that consists of auspicious qualities is possible in Viṣṇu. Thus [it is stated] in the Brahma-tarka (1.14).
Rudra is situated upon Brahmā, who is seated on a lotus throne.
As stated in the *Pādma Purāṇa* (15.18): "Brahmā rests upon Viṣṇu; Hara is seated on the lap of Brahmā; and all the gods are likewise stationed within the various limbs of Hara."

The space between heaven and earth is pervaded by You alone in a single form; this is because it has been stated that [Your] end and middle do not exist. Furthermore, the phrase "thus" is used with respect to the infinity of Your qualities. With respect to time, it is said: "By You the universe is stretched out within Your form. Anticipating the doubt that one might not perceive the end even though it exists, He says: "By You the infinite universe is stretched out. The repetition is for the purpose of making the intended meaning known. The statement "You pervade everything, therefore You are all" serves as an explanation of the word "all" in passages such as "All this, indeed, is Brahman. (19)
The universal form of Viṣṇu, which was displayed to Arjuna by the devotees residing in the three worlds, was seen according to his own fitness and its true nature.
Generally, they were with Pārtha, and generally those snakes were terrified;
through the practice of seeing him, their sight became a source of overflowing bliss.
At that time, however, it was due to his exertion for the purpose of removing the burden of the earth.
Just as there was no fear anywhere from the fierce [Arjuna] for those who perceive the Great One (Brahman),
so too there was no fear for those who were superior to Arjuna.

Because of the statement in the *Āgneya-purāṇa*, "Of Śrī, Brahmā, Rudra, and the others, [and] of Kṛṣṇa, Bhīma, and Rāma," the passage beginning with "Having seen the wondrous form" is appropriate. (19–20)
"The hosts of liberated gods enter. Regarding this, it is said in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*: "The entry and exit of the liberated ones occurs according to their own will. (21–25)

Even for those performing other actions, entry [into the mouth] is logical, just as living beings enter the waters of universal dissolution by means of the Lord’s own action alone. Furthermore, because the faces of the Lord are turned toward both sides from the midst of the army, both armies enter therein. As for those who are to die at that very moment, even though their heads are crushed between his teeth, they do not appear so to human vision because they fall within the range of subtle perception.
Just as a jar or similar object, even when broken, is not recognized by those of dull vision until it falls apart; and just as the old age of Purūravas was perceived only by the Aśvins. (26–30)
The question concerns specifically the particular qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) and action (*karman*); this is evident from the vocative address "O Viṣṇu. (31)
"Kāla is Janārdana because he possesses all perfect qualities; or because of his power of withdrawal (saṃhāra), or because of his omniscience, or because of his causing all-knowing beings to flee.
Thus it is said in the Mahāvārāha Purāṇa. By the word "api" (also/even), it is implied that one may even exclude brothers and others. (32-33)

The distinction [regarding Jayadratha] arises solely from the boon granted by his father. They have been slain or are as good as slain. Even if he stands behind Arjuna, he will certainly not kill him. (34–38)

"Vāyu [is so called] due to his connection with power and knowledge; Śaśāṅka is one who is endowed with extreme bliss; Indra is so because of supreme sovereignty—thus the Lord has various names. Thus [it is said]. (39–41)
"Even though He is the one supreme among all, He is disregarded.
And: "He alone is to be known as superior to all; for He alone performs [all things]. (42–45)
The meaning is: "Be in that very form" implies that one should manifest that [form] by concealing the various other forms.
As it is said in the Vaihāyasa-saṃhitā: "One should contemplate the five-faced one of inconceivable form, seated upon a lotus, who has concealed his universal form. (46)

"He is the Lord whose names are universal, since He is the Master endowed with perfect attributes"—thus it is said in the *Padma Purāṇa*. By the phrase "never seen before by anyone other than you," it is understood that it was seen by him [Indra] while still in his body as Indra. The expression "by anyone other than you" is used in relation to those who are inferior to you; it means that even they did not see it in that same way. "The four-faced Brahmā first beheld the Universal Form;
Rudra saw it with a hundredth part of that, and Vāsava (Indra) with a hundredth part of that."

"Just as Indra saw it in the past, Arjuna, though being [merely] Arjuna, also beheld it; others, however, by the application of gradual stages, perceive but a hundredth part and so forth of it," thus it is said in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*. (47)

Even by the Vedas and other scriptures, You cannot be seen in this manner by anyone inferior to You; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with such passages as, "Having seen the wondrous form. (48-49)

"Like one's own" means one's own form (*svakaṃ rūpam*). It does not show the universal form (*viśvarūpa*) to the ignorant as it shows its own true nature (*svarūpa*). The distinction is that this [universal form] is shown to the ignorant in exactly the same way. Otherwise, [Arjuna's request], "I wish to see Your form," would be contradictory.
However, the distinction between the higher and lower forms of the Lord—the forms of His manifestations and the universal form—is made only with respect to the vision of the deluded.
"And thus there is no distinction [between them], for manifestation is indeed relative to the ignorant. (50)
It is called "human" because it appears in some respects like a human being. || 51 ||
Even those who longed for a vision have now almost seen it. || 52 ||
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā-Tātparya-Nirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānanda Tīrtha Bhagavatpāda. || 11 ||
Now begins the twelfth chapter.

Hari Oṃ. Herein is the determination of the means: "Born for glory, he has come forth from glory; he bestows glory and vital strength upon his worshippers. Clothed in glory, they have attained immortality; their encounters become true when the measurer of the earth is present. "The consort of Viṣṇu, the mistress of the world, is the giver of liberation immediately upon being worshipped."
"She who is Śrī, Lakṣmī, Aupalā, Ambikā, and Hrī, is called the foremost consciousness and the supreme knowledge (suvidyā). From such scriptural passages as these, and from the statement:
"Śrī, when well-pleased, will very quickly produce the satisfaction of Hari."
Since dissatisfaction with that [dissatisfaction] is itself not satisfied, one should therefore always meditate upon it.
They call that unmanifest Nature (prakṛti), the immovable and the imperishable;
they also call it the Primal Matter (pradhāna) and the Great Person (mahāpuruṣa).
"Regarding that, they call it the Great Brahman, the Supreme Soul, and the Supreme Consciousness;
its supreme essence is Viṣṇu, who is the Great Brahman.

Because of this statement from the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, [Arjuna] asks out of a doubt regarding liberation through the worship of the Unmanifest (*avyakta*). The word "Unmanifest" refers to the material nature (*cit-prakṛti*), because of the subsequent statement, "The Immutable is called the Indestructible," and because it is also described as "the Immutable and the Immovable. Otherwise, the distinction in the questions—"Those who worship You," "And those who [worship] the Indestructible," and "Which of these are the best knowers of yoga?"—would be untenable.

For it has been stated by Him Himself: "You are the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Abode, and the Ultimate Purifier. As for those who claim that even though the Blessed Lord has stated in such passages as "They are considered by Me to be the most disciplined" and "Fix your mind on Me alone," that the worshippers of the Unmanifest possess superiority—they are indeed highly reckless due to their denial [of the truth] and are truly pitiable.
As it is said in the Āgneya Purāṇa: "Because one does not waver from His own state, prosperity is therefore considered immovable (acalā).
Furthermore: "On account of its subtlety, its lack of manifest renown, and likewise because of the abundance of its qualities..."
"Śrī and Mādhava are likewise indescribable, unmanifest, and inconceivable," thus it is said in the Nāradīya Purāṇa.
Even though she has been worshipped by those who do not know Viṣṇu, who are not His devotees, and who are devoid of His worship, Śrī— who knows the true nature of Him— curses them.
A devotee of her, having worshipped her, should constantly meditate upon Śrī;
being pleased by that, she shall grant him unimpeded service to Viṣṇu.
Then, by the sight of that, he attains liberation; there is no doubt in this matter.
Nevertheless, [he seeks] that which is supreme among all things and devoid of all defects.
Having known that supreme glory and its Lord, Puruṣottama,
and having realized Him, those who worship Him constantly are indeed considered the most disciplined.
For their affliction is greater when they worship Śrī separately;
indeed, when she is meditated upon together with Viṣṇu, she attains supreme satisfaction.

Furthermore, O Viṣṇu, one must contemplate Him as the Lord of Śrī without any interruption; thus, liberation will come after a long time. Therefore, let those who worship Viṣṇu attain liberation without hardship.
Thus says the supreme scripture; they are the most appropriate and the most effective means. || 2 || 3 ||
"He who does not remember anyone other than Viṣṇu, except for the sake of his service or his subordination to Him, is proclaimed as one of non-dual yoga. Furthermore,

because the worship of other deities was previously censured in such passages as, "But their fruit is finite," the question regarding the object of worship was directed specifically toward Lakṣmī, owing to her extreme proximity [to the Lord].
That man who always performs only Vaiṣṇava rites— such as recitation, worship, and purification— as well as those duties prescribed for his own specific stage of life;

That which consists of worshipping other deities and so forth, and then offering it to Hara, should be understood as not being that [true] action; rather, such a person merely possesses the yoga of that [offering].
In this regard, the former [the *smṛti*] would be superior because it is remembered as being distinguished by its beginning, middle, and end;
and because of the rule regarding the intermediate state, it is due to his [Viṣṇu’s] servitude to Him.
Even another person who engages with the mind in the remembrance of Hari according to their capacity becomes fit as previously described, provided they desire that constantly.
For one who lacks right knowledge, knowledge itself is superior to meditation;
having understood this, one should then practice meditation, free from desire for its fruits.
"Therefore, liberation arises clearly from knowledge and from renunciation joined with meditation. And: "Peace is liberation. (4-15)

He is one who has abandoned all undertakings that lead to rebirth. He is a renouncer by virtue of abandoning the egoism associated with all undertakings, by abandoning the fruits of action, and by surrendering everything to the Blessed Lord, as stated in such passages as:
"The wise declare the renunciation of the fruits of all actions to be true renunciation," and "Having surrendered all actions to Me with a mind focused on the Self."

"He who desires nothing whatsoever without devotion, knowledge, and dispassion, and who has abandoned both the auspicious and the inauspicious—he indeed is celebrated by the wise. And: "He who is generally equanimous toward pleasure and the like, and generally free from joy and the like..."
Thus it is said, just as a person with little wealth is called "destitute" by people.

"For there is no equality for anyone with respect to pleasure and pain in their primary sense, nor is there the abandonment of joy and so forth anywhere until liberation. And: "'Harṣa' is proclaimed as that which, through intoxication, leads to unrighteousness," according to the *Śabdanirṇaya*. (17–19)

[The devotees] are dear when [the means] are separate, and exceedingly dear when [the means] are combined. Devotion (*bhakti*) has already been mentioned even in the case of the separate [means]. In the verse beginning with "He from whom one does not tremble" (*yasmān nodvijate*), devotion is also implied by the word "and that" (*sa ca*). That which is a means to *dharma* is *dharmya*; that very thing which is a means to the immortal (*amṛta*) is *dharmyāmṛta*. || 20 ||
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā-Tātparya-Nirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandātman Bhagavatpāda. 12.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
Hari Oṃ. This is a summary of all matters:
"The cause of injury to the living being, that which impels it by another, and the body beginning with the unmanifest—in which this field perishes—is the field."
Desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the body, and the pervasiveness of the mind—
these should be known as its modifications, being the nature of consciousness mixed with desire and the rest.

The living being (jīva) who is freed from the desire for transformation and the like, and endowed with the desire for pure consciousness alone, is called liberated; and liberation is considered to be of two kinds.
When there is aversion toward pure consciousness and suffering toward the body— which is essentially of the nature of false vision—
and where there is a constant desire for what is prohibited, that is the demonic state of liberation.
"Devotion to Viṣṇu is indeed pure consciousness; the body consists of right vision;
and fortitude, which accords with the desire for happiness, is considered divine. Thus says the Nārāyaṇa Śruti.
"The Lord Viṣṇu is the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña); there is truly no other [field], for the field is [He] directly."
That Blessed One knows all that is to be known, being distinct from both the manifest and the unmanifest.
He, however, is established both within all living beings and outside of them;
and he is always distinct from all living beings whatsoever.
Because he possesses the power of hands, feet, and so forth everywhere, he has hands, feet, and the like in all places; indeed, Kṛṣṇa the Yādava has hair even upon his hair.
Because he exists everywhere in forms subtler than the subtle, endowed with hands, feet, and so forth,
he possesses hands and feet on all sides.
He perceives the objects of all the senses while possessing non-material (aprākṛta) senses;
therefore he is said to be "without senses" (anindriya), neither because he lacks senses nor because his senses are divided.
Devoid of qualities such as *sattva* and the rest, yet possessing the form of all that is auspicious;
he is both unmoving and indeed moving because of his freedom from the absence of manifestation.
From its movement, it is pervasive in all places; likewise, the atom is intermediate.
Because it is omnipresent, it is both near and far, as well as within.
"Because its power is infinite and inexhaustible, all qualities exist there [in Him] while being opposed elsewhere; and there, no qualities are mutually contradictory. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, the individual soul (jīva) does not possess the name *kṣetrajña*.

"The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) beholds these manifestations of the mind, which are fashioned by the Māyā of the individual soul (jīva), impermanent, appearing and disappearing; for he is pure, while the agent is impure. Thus it is said in the Bhāgavata Purāṇa.

Therefore, when it is said, "He who knows this," one might think that even the individual soul (jīva) attains that [state] through its limited knowledge; to exclude that possibility, the Lord says, "And know Me as the Knower of the Field" (kṣetrajña). Otherwise, since the point would already be established by the statement "He who knows this," the addition of "And the Knower of the Field" would be redundant. On the view of difference, however, the phrase "He who knows this" is intended to explain the etymology of the name. Furthermore, because some assert even the non-difference of all things, He negates the derivation [of the term *kṣetrajña*] as "the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower (*jña*").

The meaning is: "Know Me as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) because I abide in all fields. On that [other] view, however, since it was said "he who knows," the fact that the Lord (Īśvara) is also the Knower of the Field is already established. Furthermore, if the intention were to express non-difference from everything, one should have said "the entire field" (sarvaṃ kṣetram); saying "in the fields" (kṣetreṣu) would be redundant. Moreover, on that view, there is no particular significance for the word "Me" (mām); rather, one should have simply said "the one [field]" (eka eva kṣetraḥ). || 3 ||

And from what [it proceeds]: that from which, by the permission of the Supreme Lord, this [universe] goes forth and proceeds; and he who is the permitter. *Anumati* is a conforming cognition in the form of an impulse. As it is said: "Impulse is declared to be *anumati*; in some places it is called consent (*saṃvāda*).
But because he impels, the Blessed One is celebrated as the 'Permitter' (*anumantā*)."

And thus: by the very words "the witness and the consenter," both the consent and the consenter have been stated; and by the passage beginning with "That which is to be known," its power has also been described. (4)
Volition is the pervasion of the mind. As it is said: "The body is designated as the aggregate; volition, however, is the pervasion of the mind. (5-7)

The direct perception of Viṣṇu, who is the object of the ignorance of reality, is the "vision of the meaning of the ignorance of reality. By the etymologies "that by which something is known is knowledge" (*jñāyate 'neneti jñānam*) and "knowledge is the act of knowing" (*jñaptir jñānam*), both the means of knowledge and knowledge itself are stated in the passage, "This is declared to be knowledge. || 12 ||
When it is said that [He] is "without beginning" (anādi), a doubt might arise that He is not Himself a cause; in order to dispel that, he says "possessing no beginning" (anādimat).

And as it is said: "Because He is primarily full of all qualities, Janārdana is the Supreme Brahman; because He transcends both the formed and the formless, He is called neither existent nor non-existent."
"Because it is perceivable as having form, the existent (sat) is understood; because it is unknowable, the supreme is non-existent (asat).

Because He cannot be reached by the power of men, yet is established by all the Vedas, the Lord Viṣṇu, the imperishable, is distinct from both the existent and the non-existent. Thus [it is said]. || 17 ||

It is "to be reached through knowledge" (*jñānagamya*) because it is attained by means of knowledge. It is "knowable" (*jñeya*) because one knows oneself by oneself; for its being known by another was already established previously by the statement, "That which is the knowable. With the subsequent word "knowable," he refutes the view of those who maintain the contradiction between agent and object. [As it is said: "O Keśava, He is His own knower, His own act of knowing, and He is to be known by Himself;
yet He may be the knower of another, the cognition of another, and the object of knowledge for others at some time."
Indeed, without his grace, no one at all would be able to know [him];
for in the knowledge of himself or the knowledge of another, he does not depend on anything else.
"Therefore, the one Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) is called self-luminous (svaprakāśa).
The self-luminosity of individual souls (jīvas) is their own awareness [of Him] through His grace. Thus it is said. || 18 ||
For my state of being; for devotion toward me. || 19 ||
"Keśava knows both Prakṛti and Puruṣa, as well as his own knowledge and that which is to be known by himself;
he may at some time be the knower, the act of knowing, and the object of knowledge for others."
Indeed, without His grace, no one at all would be able to know [Him];
for in the knowledge of Himself or in the knowledge of another, He does not depend on anything else.
"Therefore, the one Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) is called 'self-luminous' (svaprakāśa);
the self-luminosity of individual souls (jīvas) is their own awareness [of Him] through His grace. Thus it is said. (18)
"Madbhāvāya" means for the sake of devotion toward me. || 19 ||

In the phrase "prakṛtiṃ puruṣaṃ ca," the word *puruṣa* is used to include both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*), while the word *prakṛti* is used to include both the conscious and unconscious primordial natures (*cetana-acetana-prakṛti*). The expression "both of them" is employed to indicate that they are the material causes (*upādāna*) of the modifications (*vikāra*), such as the *sattva* and other *guṇas*. However, independence (*svātantrya*) belongs to the Supreme Lord alone, as will be stated later in the passage beginning with "the witness, the permitter, and so forth. Furthermore, although the *guṇas* are themselves modifications, they are mentioned separately from "other modifications and the *guṇas*" because the intention is to emphasize that they constitute a higher order of modification.

That which, by means of its own actions, obscures the reality of Viṣṇu within the individual soul— the cause of the soul's own body and senses— is considered to be *prakṛti*, whose nature is to be the cause of that obscuration.
Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person and eternal creator of all, is always the one who bestows upon the individual soul the power to experience pleasure and pain.
"Just as the Lord of Vikuṇṭha is said to be the special agent of certain things, so too the Protector of All is said to be the special agent by virtue of his own action. Thus it is stated.

Although the Supreme Lord alone is the creator of everything, this is said in order to show that the Goddess has only a minor role in the granting of the capacity to enjoy [the fruits of karma]. This is stated in both places. Even regarding the status of being the agent, He alone is the primary cause.

Nevertheless, because its activity is more extensive with respect to the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*), it is said that "primordial matter (*prakṛti*) is called the cause in [the matter of] agency. Thus, although Viṣṇu is the cause of everything, primordial matter has only a limited activity in bestowing the state of being an enjoyer upon the individual soul (*jīva*); therefore, the person (*puruṣa*) is called the "cause in [the matter of] enjoyment. This is stated as a specific cause. However, the intended meaning is that, primarily, the status of being the cause of everything belongs to Viṣṇu alone. In the verse "The person situated in primordial matter," the word *puruṣa* refers to the individual soul, since both [the Supreme Person and the individual soul] were previously introduced by the term *puruṣa*, and because the interpretation is appropriate according to what fits each case. (21)

In order to refute those who claim that the relationship between cause and effect and experience (*bhoga*) are false, he says: "For *prakṛti* resides in the *puruṣa*. The word "for" (*hi*) demonstrates the contradiction with experience for them. Indeed, the falsity of internal experience—whose objects are knowledge, ignorance, pleasure, pain, and so forth—is never observed anywhere. Nor is there any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its falsity. For it is only from the body onwards that perceptual error (*aparokṣabhrama*) is observed. Even in those cases, its status as an error must be inferred solely due to contradiction with a stronger means of valid cognition.
