If one were to accept that even what is established by a witness is an error, then for one who has understood that everything is either an error or non-error, the very self would be the authority [for that understanding]. Even from the perspective of worldly convention (*vyavahāra*), neither error nor non-error can be established. If it is said that "experience is erroneous," how could its erroneousness, or the validity of that [statement], be established?

If it is argued that "we accept everything from the standpoint of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*)," then from where are convention and the conventional agent themselves established? If it is argued that they are established "from cognition (*pratīti*)," then from where is that very cognition established? If it is argued that it is "self-established (*svataḥ*)," then if the self is erroneous, there would be the error of thinking that cognition exists even without being cognized; it would also follow that it is its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); and the notion that "it exists by itself" would be a delusion. Furthermore, since an objectless delusion is untenable, this [self-establishment] must also be established as a delusion; thus, even that which is considered a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is in fact not a valid means of knowledge.

If it is claimed that there is an illusion regarding its being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), nothing at all is established. If this very [cognition] is an illusion, then everything else must necessarily be non-illusory. Since the cognition whose object is pleasure, pain, and so forth is the very nature of the Self (*ātmasvarūpa*), if that were illusory, the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*) would follow without even a pretext. For even for them [the Buddhists], ignorance (*ajñāna*) and the like do not have the cognition of a mental modification (*vṛtti-jñāna*) as their object. Furthermore, since it is accepted that an illusion is an effect of ignorance (*avidyā*), the nature of the Self itself would consequently become an effect of ignorance.

To the statement that "difficult-to-establish-ness (*durghaṭatva*) is an ornament," the reply is: "For us, both difficult-to-establish-ness and easy-to-establish-ness (*sughaṭatva*) are ornaments. Indeed, no exception has ever been observed against something established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), whether it be difficult to establish or not. Since those who claim that "difficult-to-establish-ness is an ornament" have themselves accepted the nature of ignorance (*avidyātva*), why is its status as an ornament not likewise accepted when it is argued that "that [ignorance] is untenable"?

Because [their position] is extremely easy to refute, there is no need for a further response from those who claim that even the self (*ātman*) is ignorance (*avidyā*). Therefore, because it is tainted by infinite defects, they have been rejected by the Blessed One through the very word "for" (*hi*), which indicates what is well-known. || 22 ||

He states that attachment to the qualities (guṇas) such as *sattva* is the cause for this living being’s births in good and evil wombs, whereas the independent cause is indeed the Supreme Lord alone, saying: "The witness, the consenter...
[and] "...he impels all according to his own favor through His will."
The unborn Lord Hari himself declared,
"I authorize [it]," because Viṣṇu possesses great power (mahāśakti), he is thus called Maheśvara.
"And because of His supremacy, He alone is said to be the permissive witness;
He alone, as the distinct indweller within all bodies, is the embodied one.
And [it is said]: "Know Me in all fields. Thus, even though He is spoken of in relation to the body, He shows that He Himself is that [Supreme Self]. 23.
The person who, having correctly understood both the two-fold Puruṣa and the two-fold Prakṛti along with their respective qualities, perceives them as they are—
even while moving about in every way— is not born again. || 24 ||
Because of the difference in the fitness for non-attachment, there is a means for the vision [of truth] for men.
Indeed, through the grace of Viṣṇu alone, the Vaiṣṇava form is there;
something is known by oneself, and something else is heard from another source.
Having thus known and meditated upon Hari, some sages perceive Him within their own hearts,
while other sages, such as Nārada and others, perceive Him even outside.
By the grace of Viṣṇu, through the power of true intuition they had obtained, the gods understood everything in due order, following the sequence of the clarity of their intuition.
They behold Viṣṇu both externally and internally even without meditation;
for those whose vision exists without meditation, there is indeed perception even during meditation.
They are the gods of Sāṅkhya and Yoga, and among them, Brahmā is superior.
But some excellent kṣatriyas, being devoted, were performing sacrifices such as the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) when [the Lord] arrived for his share of the sacrifice.
And by means of both hearing and intuition, they remember the Supreme Person;
likewise, others see Him after having heard everything from various sources and having assented to it.
Indeed, they perceive [the truth] only by means of worship, and never otherwise;
beginning with the sages and the kings, intuitive insight increases progressively.
Up to the realm of Brahmā, there is generally nothing that remains unmanifest to Brahmā;
for the sake of Viṣṇu’s pleasure, this [teaching] of Hari should generally be heard.
Knowledge arises for others through hearing; this is the sequence up to the Mānuṣottara mountain.
Because their intuitive insight is extremely limited, humans are merely those who know what they have heard.
"Therefore, all of them, by the mere sight of Him, go to liberation according to their own fitness.

And: although others may also possess some degree of hearing [the teachings], because human beings have extremely limited intellectual capacity (*pratibhāna*), the qualification "having heard from others" is used. Since the intuition (*pratibhā*) of humans generally does not arise correctly—being dependent on a primary means of knowledge (*mūla-pramāṇa*) and being meager—they are described as "devoted to sacred revelation" (*śrutiparāyaṇāḥ*). [As it is said:
"He whose intuition, though not based on what has been heard, is not in conflict with the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*..."
One should know that he who is born among men as one renowned is the best of gods.
A man whose body is nine times the measure of his own face,
and a woman who possesses eight such measures, are both ninety-six finger-breadths in height.
One should know that those two best of gods are ten *tālas* and seven *pādas* in height;
beyond that, the measurement of the deity gradually decreases by five finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
The foot [of the gods] is one finger-breadth less than that; it is reduced by four finger-breadths for each successive level down to the gods and secondary gods.
Again, as many finger-breadths as are subtracted from the foot [of the gods], so great shall be the measure of humans; below that, the measurement of the Asuras is traditionally taught.
Therefore, forty-two [finger-breadths] below that ninety-six-finger [measurement].
That [measurement] should clearly be known as finger-breadths (aṅgula) among the secondary gods and others;
for the ṛṣis and universal monarchs (cakravartins), it should be understood as being like that of the lower gods.

"To the extent that he is dear to Viṣṇu, to that same extent he possesses a resemblance to Hari in the form of both male and female, which remains firmly established through the beginningless succession. Thus [it is said]. (25–26)

Regarding the phrase "from the union of the field and the knower of the field," here "the field" (kṣetra) is Śrī, because it will be stated later: "My womb is the Great Brahman; in that I place the seed.
Furthermore: "The unmanifest, the Great Brahman, the Pradhāna, and the field—these are said to be Śrī, who is eternally dear to Viṣṇu and consists of flawless consciousness."
For she is not manifested; Viṣṇu dwells here, possessing great qualities, and she is the supreme soul (jīvottamā). Therefore, she is designated by these names as Akā.
He is the Great Brahmā, the Great Life-force; He is Śiva, by whom this individual soul (jīva), impelled by the Supreme Self, will think, "I am the doer."
He is called Ahaṃkāra because he performs the ego-function for the individual soul (jīva);
Umā is to be known as Buddhi because she bestows the knowledge of sound and other objects.
The mind is designated as Manu, and Indra is its son Skanda;
the ear is Candra because it causes one to hear, and touch is Marut, the son of Vāyu.
The eye is the sun because it causes things to be seen; the tongue is the lord of waters because it tastes;
the nose is the two Aśvins because it smells; and speech is Agni because of its speaking.
The two Maruts, Hāni and Ābha, should be known as the sons of Vāyu;
while Yajña and Śambhu, the sons of Śacī, have Viṣṇu presiding over their feet.
From the very act of stepping, he is the anus; from the dissolution of what has been consumed, he is Yama;
from the presence of the lineage [of progeny], he is the organ of generation, the mantra Śiva.
Vināyaka is likewise Ākāśa (Space), because it manifests through being unobstructed. The elemental wind born from the primary wind is named Marīcika.
Agni and Pṛthivī are well-known; Varuṇa is water. Their designations arise from the reasons of eating, expanding, and being the cause of birth and dissolution.
The five beginning with sound are born of Śiva;
they are so designated because of sounding, touching, as well as seeing, tasting, and smelling.
Because it is pleasure, stability, and volition, because it leads through pleasure and through stability,
and because it is the leader of the mind, Vāyu and Sarasvatī are indeed primary.
If Śrī is will (*icchā*), she herself is considered the consort of Vāyu; thus she is regarded as *ghṛti*.
Through the granting of will, she is indeed will itself, yet she appears as various deities due to differences in location.
Lakṣmī and the others are also described individually as having arisen;
moreover, Duḥkha, Dveṣa, Kali, and Dvāpara are the sons of Brahmā.
The two foremost among the Asuras were Saṅghāta and Cetana;
whatever else was desired by them was designated by their respective names.
All this, whether conscious or unconscious, is declared to be the field (kṣetra);
because it is the ground (kṣiti) of the Blessed One, it is therefore called the field.
Because it destroys and protects, it is therefore called a field (*kṣetra*);
or because it makes [the ground] firm and protects, it is thus declared a field.
"From this [it] is exhausted, by this it is saved"—
thus, moreover, another name for those fields known as Icchā and the rest is remembered.
They are called "transformations" (vikāra) because they abide as specific modifications;
and because the final effect is produced from them as a specific [modification], it is called a transformation.
Furthermore, because here [in this state] there is no activity apart from destruction,
the egoistic subjects such as Will (icchā) and the rest are designated as "modifications" only through their connection with that [destruction].
"Haristhe Kṣetrajña knows all this at all times, impelling it with his very faultless eye.

And because of such scriptural passages as "Whose self is the body," it is logical that even for a conscious being, the designation "body" is applied in statements such as "This body, O son of Kuntī."
In some places *sattva* is said to be the individual soul (*jīva*), and in others *sattva* is Janārdana;
in some instances *sattva* is a quality (*guṇa*), and in others it is called goodness (*sādhutva*).

Thus it is stated in the *Śabdanirṇaya*. Furthermore, the *Paiṅgi-śruti* says: "One of the two eats the sweet fruit; this is the *sattva*. And since the verbal root *jan* means "to manifest," the birth of the individual soul (*jīva*) in a body is also logical from the perspective of its manifestation. || 27 ||
"Even while living beings perish in the form of association with suffering and so forth, [He] remains otherwise than that:
'Even while living beings perish in the form of association with suffering and so forth,
He who is devoid of association with suffering and the like abides within all living beings.'"
"He who perceives Viṣṇu as always equal in all qualities, never deficient even when residing in an inferior state—he alone shall not enter into darkness. Thus it is said in the Padma Purāṇa (28–29).

These [actions] are initiated by Viṣṇu himself through his own nature; there is no one other than Viṣṇu who is the prior impeller, according to the Lord’s own statement: "But Bādarāyaṇa [holds that the Lord is the cause], because of the designation of a cause," and also: "Substance, action, and time... Furthermore: "The Blessed One himself creates the entire universe through his own nature;
there is no agent whatsoever for Hari, and therefore Keśava is not a non-agent."

And thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa. That [the Supreme Lord] is the agent is established simply by virtue of being the subject under discussion. Otherwise, there would be contradiction with all the authoritative scriptures (pramāṇas), such as: "I am the source of all," "For He is the agent," "The agent, the Lord, the Person, the womb of Brahman," "From whom the birth, etc., of this [world proceed]," and "Know them to be from Me alone. Furthermore, in the phrase "and by Prakṛti alone" (prakṛtyaiva ca), the word "ca" (and) establishes that it is indeed by Him [the Lord]. As it is said: "The word 'ca' may in some instances indicate connection with the subject at hand;
in some it expresses conjunction; and in some it denotes rarity."

Thus, in the *Śabdanirṇaya*, the agency of *prakṛti* (primordial nature) has been refuted by the words of the Blessed Lord, such as: "And because the arrangement is not possible, there is no inference [of a creator]" (*racanānupapatteśca nānumānam*), and also: "Nothing whatsoever is done without You" (*na ṛte tvatkriyate kiñcanāre*). Furthermore, if the agency were attributed to *prakṛti* alone, the word "and" (*ca*) would be redundant. Moreover, there would be a contradiction with the supplementary statement: "And from that very [Lord] comes the expansion" (*tata eva ca vistāram*). There is also a contradiction with what is stated here regarding the union of the field and the knower of the field (*kṣetrakṣetrajña-saṃyoga*), which is the subject at hand, and with what will be said later: "I am the father who provides the seed" (*ahaṃ bījapradaḥ pitā*).

Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with your own statement that [the Lord] makes the insentient act. The Paiṅgi Śruti states: "Agency in its primary sense is said to be the undertaking of action preceded by will. However, agency characterized as modification is indeed admitted to belong to *prakṛti*. Nevertheless, since that [primary agency] is absent in the liberated activities of Lakṣmī and the Supreme Lord, the term "in every respect" (*sarvaśaḥ*) would result in being restricted.
[As stated: "Action resting upon the insentient is said to be of the nature of modification;
whereas that which resides solely in consciousness is established by the authority of *pratyabhijñā* (recognition)."
"That which is to be known as unchanging in nature cannot be of the nature of primordial matter (prakṛti). Thus it is said. (30)

"And he who perceives the very distinction among individual souls (jīvas) residing in the one Viṣṇu, as well as their mutual differences according to their gradations, and [perceives] the world as the expansion of Viṣṇu alone—he is liberated. Thus it is said. (31)

The individual soul (jīva) resides in the body. As the Śruti declares: "Having cast off the bodily [self] through sleep, being himself unslumbering, he looks down upon those who sleep. Furthermore: "But the transmigrating soul is considered to reside in the body due to its identification with the body;
whereas Viṣṇu, although present within the body, is not said to reside in the body."
Since he never has any identification with the body,
the connection with the sufferings residing therein is what is called "identification" (abhimati).
Due to the absence of that [identification], the Blessed One, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), is not subject to such identification.

And thus: because He is beginningless and devoid of qualities, the Supreme Self is not even the *jīva* (individual soul), let alone the insentient (*jaḍa*). The distinction is that the Supreme has no beginning, characterized as the arising of a body, whereas the *jīva* indeed possesses such a beginning. Furthermore, there is the connection with qualities such as *sattva*. Although the Supreme Self performs everything, He is nevertheless untouched by it. This negation is established precisely because it is well-known among disputants, as in the passage: "They consider sacrifice and charity to be the highest. Since He performs everything yet is not tainted by merit or sin, He is free from birth, death, and the like, and is devoid of the qualities of *sattva* and so forth.
"Viṣṇu, however, is the opposite of that; therefore, the individual soul (jīva) and He are always distinct. And also: "This one is 'not this, not this' (neti neti)," and so forth. (Verses 32–34)
The liberation of living beings from the insentient primordial nature (prakṛti) is the liberation from the material nature of the elements. || 35 ||
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-gītā-tātparya-nirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānanda-tīrtha Bhagavat-pāda. || 13 ||
Hari Om. Having first clarified the union of the field (kṣetra) and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), [the Lord] now demonstrates the three qualities (traiguṇya) by means of analysis. 1–2.

"The yogin, the wife, as well as the place, the womb, and the cause"—thus it is stated in the *Śabdanirṇaya*. Here, "the womb" (*yoni*) refers to the wife, because of the supplementary statement: "In her I place the embryo. (3-15)

When he perceives the Lord as a creator distinct from these qualities such as *sattva* and the rest, only then is this person (*nā*) truly a man; otherwise, he is equal to a beast. He does not merely perceive that creator Viṣṇu as being other than himself, but also as superior to the qualities. How is it that he alone is a man? Because he attains my own state of being. "She who is known as Mahālakṣmī, the supreme consort of Nārāyaṇa, is to be understood as *prakṛti* (Nature), for she acts with pre-eminence."
That [Prakṛti] has three forms: Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas. At the time of creation, they become differentiated; Sattva is Śrī, the radiance of the virtuous qualities.
Rajas is so called because it causes coloring; it is the Earth (bhū), since it is that which performs creation. It is through its penetration that this earth is called "bhūmi."
Because she causes the exhaustion of living beings, Durgā is celebrated as "Darkness" (tamas);
by these three [qualities], all living beings are bound and do not attain liberation.
They bind everyone, yet they do so especially: Śrī binds men, while Bhū likewise binds the Daityas.
By knowing Viṣṇu as distinct from these and as supreme, one is liberated;
yet because of their preeminent power, there exists nothing higher than them.
"As long as one perceives [them] in this way, so long is that person known as a beast among men.
Therefore, Viṣṇu should always be understood as possessing qualities superior to these. Thus it is stated in the Mahāviṣṇupurāṇa, 16.19.
Regarding the statement "the fruit of *rajas*, however, is suffering," here "suffering" refers to pleasure mixed with suffering.
As stated in the *Śabdanirṇaya*: "The syllable *duḥ* is declared to mean 'suffering' (*duḥkha*), while *kha* is said to mean 'pleasure' (*sukha*).
Thus, it is taught that the fruit of *rājasa* action is pleasure mixed with suffering.
"The wise know that the fruit of the tamasic person is eternal suffering born of ignorance," thus it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa (20–21).
He generally neither hates nor desires the external luminaries that abide in the world; yet,
though he is self-luminous and free from delusion,
he still desires the external light of Viṣṇu and serves it with constant devotion.
Even in the presence of pleasure, pain, and the like, he is always equanimous in his devotion to Viṣṇu;
neither for the sake of wealth, nor for the sake of what is dear, nor even out of fear of censure and the like.
"There is no decline in his devotion to Viṣṇu; rather, there is equality or even advancement.
Avoiding undertakings that do not concern Vaiṣṇavas, he goes to Viṣṇu—of this there is no doubt. Thus it is said. || 22 ||

And because of the statement "as if indifferent," it is not mere indifference [that is meant]. The phrase "he does not stir" prohibits the activity of one who is indifferent. The expression "one who has renounced all undertakings" implies that even with regard to specific purposes, there is no undertaking of what is not Vaiṣṇava.
As stated in the *Śabdanirṇaya*: "Stirring is momentary action; a long-term undertaking is called an *ārambha*. (23–25)

And as it is said in the *Pravṛtti*: "The wise man who transcends here that beginningless bondage of the person (puruṣa) created by Lakṣmī and the others—he is to be known as one who has transcended the qualities (guṇātyayī). Because he has transcended the bondage created by them and has attained Viṣṇu, who is superior to them, he is called "one who has transcended them. It is just as when one says, "He goes to the king, passing by the doorkeeper."
"Brahmabhūyam" means becoming one with Brahman. Here, "Brahman" refers to Mahālakṣmī as the subject under discussion, according to the passage:
"Having transcended the three forms, he attains Mahālakṣmī;
favored by her, that Vaiṣṇava becomes one who goes to Viṣṇu."

He says, "One who has attained Brahman has indeed attained Me," [in the verse beginning] "For [from] Brahman... The meaning is that because of its non-separation from Me, she (Brahman) also remains situated in Me alone. Nevertheless, that statement was made with the intention of describing the sequence for attaining Me. [This refers to] the exclusive happiness that is liberation.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-gītā-tātparya-nirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānanda-tīrtha Bhagavat-pāda. 14.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter.
Hari, Oṃ. He demonstrates by analyzing what was stated in the thirteenth chapter: "Lord Hari is the distinct root of that world-tree, like the earth;
the material nature consisting of consciousness and unconsciousness, joined with the qualities of goodness (sattva) and the rest, constitutes the portion of the roots."
Here too, the union of consciousness and unconsciousness is proclaimed to be like that of a tree;
the earth-deity is like the wood, while Hari is like the clay, the unconscious element.
Because its roots are supreme, this [tree] is remembered as having its roots above;
from it descend the lower things—the intellects of "greatness" and "I-ness," conjoined with the elements.
The Vedic branches are its leaves; for from it come the fruits of desire and liberation.
Abiding in the causes, it acts as the cause; pervading the effects, it is the cause.
The branches and roots are always interconnected with one another;
because they are beautiful to behold, the sense objects are considered to be like tender sprouts. (2)
This world-tree is indeed the Aśvattha, for its nature is as flickering as a horse;
yet it is imperishable in its flow, O Viṣṇu, until it is constantly severed by the weapon of knowledge regarding one's own attachment, through the correct perception of distinctness.
But [the Self] does not set like the unmanifest and so forth, according to such scriptural statements as "Not this, not this."
O Viṣṇu, by means of awakening alone, that Keśava must be sought apart from all the multitude of living beings, including Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, and the rest. (3-4)
On account of even a slight similarity, one who is distinct is spoken of as if it were a part.
But when the Lord, the Master, enters this body, He draws toward Himself the senses, with the mind as the sixth, which had been situated in their respective sources. (5.7)
Then, when it departs from here taking the living soul along with sound and the other [objects],
it goes forth having grasped these, just as the wind carries fragrances from their source.
Established in the senses, the Lord experiences auspicious enjoyments;
for although the Blessed One is full of bliss, he indeed experiences them through his divine play.
Because of his gentleness, he is named Soma; he is always associated with the essence of the moon.
That very same Viṣṇu, when established as fire, is always known by the name Vaiśvānara. He is indeed that upon which all living beings always depend for their livelihood.
He alone, in the form of Vyāsa, is proclaimed as the author of the Vedānta. || 15 ||
Brahmā, Rudra, and all others are perishable because their bodies are subject to decay;
whereas Śrī is declared to be of an imperishable nature because her body consists of eternal consciousness.
Furthermore, she is so called because she is the sustainer of this entire aggregate of the sentient and the insentient.
The immutable Self is to be known as the Supreme Self, Hari himself. || 16-17 ||

"Because he is eternally superior to these two, whose natures are the perishable and the imperishable, he is therefore renowned in both the world and the Veda by the name Puruṣottama. Thus says the Nārāyaṇa Śruti (18–20).
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā-Tātparya-Nirṇaya*, composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānanda Tīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.
Hari Oṃ. The characteristics of gods and asuras:
"Those who, out of excessive pride, think, 'I am the Supreme Lord,' [are mistaken];
this entire world is false because it does not endure due to its origin in delusion."
Because of its falsity, God does not exist; nor is He born from others, nor likewise from Himself or another, when it is said that He is the controller and the end.
But at the end of the asuras, they all go to the lowest darkness because of their desire for lordship over the unworthy, and because of greed in surrendering themselves.
Because they harbor hatred toward those who know reality, darkness is not difficult for them to attain;
for they contradict perception, scripture, inference, and even their own words.
Therefore, they should be known as asuras, and others of that kind are likewise so.

"But those who, knowing Viṣṇu to be supreme, worship no other deity, go to liberation solely through knowledge that is non-contradictory to perception and other means of valid cognition. Thus it is said in the *Brahmavaivarta*. "For bondage" means for the sake of binding in a low place, in blinding darkness.
"Even though there are a great many creations, two are preeminent in terms of their auspicious and inauspicious fruits."
"Only two [classes] are called gods and asuras; the gandharvas and others are included within them.

Those who go to liberation are to be known as gods alone, for they are those who have attained final release. And because of the prefix *vi-* in the word *vimokṣāya* (for the sake of liberation), the multiplicity of types of liberation is understood.
The states of being gods, asuras, humans, and so forth, belong to living beings by their very nature;
this nature cannot be altered by anyone or anywhere.
It was solely by the power of a curse that the gods attained the state of Prahlāda and others;
therefore, they shall once again return to their own original divinity.
This alteration occurs due to a cause, just as redness appears in a crystal;
therefore, it is not eternal, nor does it involve the actual cessation of the intrinsic nature.
"But having indeed overcome that [state], he should remain; for from that comes the divine creation.
He is to be known as truly beyond grief, fit for liberation, and dear to Hari. Thus [it is said]. 1.24.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavadgītā-tātparya-nirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānanda-tīrtha Bhagavat-pāda. || 16 ||
Now begins the seventeenth chapter.
Hari Oṃ. Discernment between Good and Evil Actions. 1-2.

It conforms to the *sattva* and conforms to the individual soul (*jīva*). Therefore, those whose faith is characterized by *sattva* (sāttvika) should be known as *sāttvika*, as distinguished from others. It consists of faith; its very nature is faith.
"Faith is the nourishment of the soul; therefore, according to the distinctions of faith, souls should be known individually as superior, inferior, or middling."
For those who have attained liberation from the darkness and for those remaining in the cycle of transmigration, it is faith alone that remains as their essential nature;
however, for others, there remains a mind whose form is faith.

In that regard, the faith of one who is predominantly *sāttvika* is generally manifested as being of the very nature of their own essence; however, in some cases, even for a *tāmasa* person, there may be a faith within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) that takes the form of *tamas*.
Because of the predominance of that [quality], it is distinguished as *sāttvika* [faith] even in such a person. (3)
Faith is said to be the steadfastness of conviction toward those who are the supreme deities.
Those who perceive Viṣṇu with the same devotion as they do for his devotees, and likewise for Ramā, Brahmā, and others, should be known as sāttvika; for by them, Viṣṇu alone is truly worshipped.
Śrī, Sādhyakṣavidyā, and the deities beginning with Brahmā and Indra—
known as Manus because of their divine nature— enjoy [the offerings] with affection.
But those who perform mixed sacrifices, yet harbor doubts regarding the superiority of Viṣṇu,
while always possessing faith in the mere individual forms of the gods;
They should be known as rājasa; by them, the yakṣas and rākṣasas were worshipped.
Due to their wretchedness, they are called "devas," though their names are actually Brahmā, Indra, and so forth.
Those who grasp Hari as being exactly equal to other deities and the like,
or who consider Him to be inferior, or even think that He is not the unsurpassed Brahman and so forth— [they do not know Him].
Then, at the end of that [period], those possessed of faith were proclaimed as the Tāmasas;
by them were worshipped the Bhūtas and Pretas, who bear names such as Śiva, Skanda, and others.
Indeed, those who are excessively tamasic eat as the direct retinue of Śiva;
their fruits are, respectively, liberation, heaven according to one's will, and the state of being a Bhūta or similar spirit.
Even having abandoned what is prescribed by the scriptures, those who are free from false knowledge worship Viṣṇu with devotion, avoiding the performance of prohibited acts.
Even they go to Hari if they abide by the injunctions of the scriptures; how much more so those people who perform terrible austerities not ordained by the scriptures?
Endowed with hypocrisy and egoism, and possessed by the force of desire and passion.
Even though the gods, such as Lakṣmī and others, are not emaciated, those who are devoted to Viṣṇu perceive them— and Viṣṇu himself who dwells within all bodies— as being emaciated.
Because you conceive of them as having few virtues, you will certainly go to hell; and those Daityas, Piśācas, or Rākṣasas shall be known [as such].
Moreover, these men for the most part become sattvic through food, sacrifices, and other such acts; because they make others sattvic as well, while others likewise [make them] otherwise.
"Oṃ tat sat"—these three names of Viṣṇu which have been proclaimed are well-known in the Veda; therefore, ritual action is indeed real only when it has them as its object.
In that regard, what is performed without faith is proclaimed as "non-existent" (asat),
because from it the Brahmins, the Vedas, and the sacrifices are mutually woven together.
He was ordained by that Viṣṇu, and thus he is celebrated as "Viṣṇu-roma"; and because all this is woven within him, he is called "Om."

Therefore, the followers of the Vedas indeed commence sacrifices and other rites with "Oṃ"; for that which is not preceded by "Oṃ" would be demonic, whereas that which is preceded by "Oṃ" is [divine].

From a complete lack of knowledge regarding the meaning of the syllable *Aṃ*, the fruit becomes demonic; however, when performed without any ulterior motive, that very act becomes Brahman, my own abode.
Because the action is performed in this manner, Janārdana is named accordingly;
for he is said to be either "intent upon" (abhisaṃhita) that [action] or "pervaded" (tata) by his own qualities at all times.

And so forth. In the *Śabdanirṇaya*, it is stated: "I have described the Pradhāna, its essential nature, and its effects. Furthermore, he will state that even that which is prescribed by the scriptures is as good as non-existent if it is devoid of faith in the Lord, in the verse beginning, "That which is offered without faith... It is precisely because of the absence of faith in the Lord that something becomes contrary to the scriptures. The *Paiṅgi Śruti* declares: "The entire scripture proceeds for the purpose of enjoining devotion to Viṣṇu. (4–7)

*Sthira* (stable) substances are those possessing stable qualities, such as ghee and the like. Even pungent (*kaṭu*) and other [flavors] are indeed *sāttvika* when they serve the purpose of health, vitality, and so forth. Conversely, even delicious (*rasya*) and other [flavors] are *rājasa* when they are causes of ill-health and the like, because it is said: "They bestow suffering, grief, and disease. *Sattva* is the state of goodness; for that too arises from pure food. As it is said: "That which is pleasing to the heart, charming later on, dear, and giving pleasure at the moment is [merely] pleasant;
but that which gives long-term happiness and pleasure through repeated practice is truly *rasya*."
Thus ends [the section on] the determination of words. || 8 ||
Rūkṣa is sapless; tīkṣṇa refers to mustard seeds and the like. || 9 ||
"That which has undergone digestion after a lapse of time is called *yātayāma*;

in some cases it may be *gatasāra* (devoid of essence), while that which has been consumed is *yātamasya*. And: "That which was sweet before but subsequently becomes otherwise is *gatarasa* (devoid of flavor)."
"But for pure Bhāgavatas, one should understand the sweetness and other qualities of substances solely in relation to their own nature, and not otherwise," so it is said in the *Sūdaśāstra*. (10–11)
From the Rājasūya sacrifice, however, heaven is declared to be attained through mere intention;
it is a world belonging to the gods along with the distressed, sharing names such as Vāsava and others.

For those who lack faith in Viṣṇu and desire unworthy objects, there shall be rebirth; and those characterized by passion (rājasa), who go to the world of men, fall into hell unless they perform sacrifice.
If they should perform prohibited actions, they would certainly go to hell;
yet sometimes those of a sattvic nature may perform actions that are rajasic or tamasic.
Although they are distinct from one another, their state remains nonetheless natural;
yet for all of them, each respective action shall always bear great fruit.
"Furthermore, there is little fruit, and the characteristic among them is abundance. Thus it is stated in the Padma Purāṇa, 12.15.
Mauna is reflection. || 16 ||

"By those who are disciplined" means by those disciplined in yoga such as dedication to the Lord (bhagavadarpaṇa) and so forth. "By those who are disciplined" applies equally to all [virtues] such as giving and the rest. Because of its connection with the Real (sat), action and the other [virtues] are themselves real (sat). (17–22)

Because the phrase "Oṃ tat sat" is well-known as the names of Viṣṇu; and because of the Vedic scripture stating, "The Brahman that is not preceded by Oṃ flows away, and it perishes thereafter; an action not preceded by Oṃ is demonic," there is the established tradition that what is not preceded by Oṃ is demonic. Furthermore: "A mantra uttered by one ignorant of its purpose protects the reciter only in vain."

And from the Paiṅgi Śruti: "Whatever mantra is recited by him, that alone is to be known as the meaning of the mantra. Furthermore, because action performed without the desire for fruits is *sāttvika* precisely due to being for the sake of that [the Lord], the sense is that through devotion to Him, action preceded by remembrance of Him is truly real (*sat*), while any other is indeed unreal (*asat*). Even *rājasa* action is included within the unreal, because it is devoid of faith in Viṣṇu. As it is said: "Sāttvika action bestows liberation; rājasa action bestows the suffering of worldly transmigration."
"That which is characterized by tamas should be known as leading to downfall; one should indeed perform that action which is Vaiṣṇava. Thus, in the Āgneya-purāṇa, verses 23–28.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-gītā-tātparya-nirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānanda-tīrtha Bhagavat-pāda. || 17 ||
Now begins the eighteenth chapter.

Hari Om. This [chapter] consists of a summary of the determination of the duties taught in all the preceding chapters, and it also teaches the doctrine of the three gunas not previously mentioned. 1–2.

Since they have been described as "wise," they too are beyond reproach. Therefore, the meaning of the statement "that which is tainted by defects should be abandoned" is: "having abandoned attachment and the fruit [of action]. (3–4)

The meaning is that among the sacrifices of material substances (dravyayajña) and so forth, each person should perform the sacrifice appropriate to them; likewise, among the gifts of knowledge (vidyādāna) and so forth, one should give the gift appropriate to oneself, and likewise perform the austerity (tapas) appropriate to oneself—all those belonging to the various stages of life (āśrama), as well as others. For the lowest castes, the recitation of the names of Viṣṇu constitutes study (svādhyāya), and for them, fasting (upavāsa) and other such practices constitute austerity (tapas). (5–6)

"Out of the delusion known as false knowledge, one thinks that the abandonment of one's own nature must be performed apart from the renunciation of the fruits of action; for it is said in the *Padma Purāṇa*: 'Having abandoned their own sacrifices and other duties, they undoubtedly go to hell. (7)
"Without delusion, it is simply the suffering that has been perceived. By the word "suffering," only mental [suffering] is meant, because physical affliction is mentioned separately.
As stated in the *Śabdanirṇaya*: "Mental suffering is to be known as *duḥkha*, while external exertion is called *āyāsa*; this is when a distinction is intended, otherwise everything [is both]. (8–9)
The sattvic person does not hate unwholesome karma merely because it yields suffering in the present life;
nor does he become attached to merit performed in other births, for he is steady.
For one who knows the true reality of Viṣṇu and performs action solely with the intention of offering it to Him,
being devoid of desire for the fruit, that action shall not lead to bondage.
"And: 'If [an action] is abundant and its fault is slight, so long as it is seen by one who has direct perception. (10–11)

This is desired by others, but for him [the knower], it is not desired precisely because of his renunciation (tyāgitva). As it is said: "There can be no fruit of action other than knowledge and the like, or that which is to be enjoyed in liberation"; and also: "For the renouncer who knows reality, there is no fruit other than that. Thus, the distinction of *saṃnyāsa* (renunciation) from mere *tyāga* (abandonment) is that it involves the non-performance even of purely optional (*kāmya*) rites due to a lack of expectation for results; therefore, those who are not renouncers are mentioned as the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) to the renunciants. For even they possess renunciation, insofar as they do not perform optional rites anywhere, even at the request of others.
"And those who are renunciants (nyāsinaḥ) are superior to others who have renounced the fruits [of action]. Thus it is said. || 12 ||
The basis (adhiṣṭhāna) consists of the body and so forth. || 14-16 ||
"The ignorant person perceives sovereignty only in the Lord and never in the Self;
for them, the sovereignty of the Self exists solely as dependent upon the Lord."
Regarding the gradations of fortune and so forth for all living beings in every respect,
he who has arisen for that purpose— just as Rudra or Yama—
is not slain and is not bound, even after destroying these worlds.
Even though born for that purpose, the ignorant person is certainly slain like a demon;
whereas he who possesses direct vision is not born again for the sake of that happiness which leads to liberation.

"One who knows [the truth] beyond his perception should diminish [his power]; he is tainted only slightly by a fault. Thus it is said. Because he knows his lack of independence, he does not even have the thought "I shall kill," and so he does not kill. This is the distinction: another person possesses such a thought. As it is said, "He whose intellect is not tainted"—he does not kill out of passion, but rather with a sense of duty (*dharma*).
"For one who considers himself independent, acting out of passion while performing what is considered duty..."
"But the defect would have that as its cause, while the quality would arise from one's own karma. Thus it is said. || 17 ||
"The impulse of the Lord, the Impeller, which consists of the knower, the known, and the act of knowing, impels all conscious beings toward their actions; for that impulse is He Himself."
By its very nature it is eternal, yet it exists as a particular;
likewise, the particular is also eternal by its very nature, yet it exists through its particularity.
Because it is self-sustaining, there is no infinite regress, just as in the case of a qualified entity;
for the particular (viśeṣa) certainly exists here, and there is never any infinite regress. Indeed, no one has the experience of thinking, "I am other than the knower."
"I am indeed known"—from this [notion] how could there be a distinction between those two?
This specific [thought], "I see," has now arisen for me.
From such experiences as these, there is no difference between the qualified object and its qualifier;
however, the qualifier is of two kinds: that which is called a "particular" (viśeṣa) and the other.
"That by which a distinction is brought about is called a qualifier;
even a distinction serves as the indicator of itself.

Thus it is stated in the *Tattvaviveka*. "Compendium" (*saṅgraha*) refers to the summary of the five causes, since the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is included within the instrument (*karaṇa*). Because the Lord, denoted by the word "destiny" (*daiva*), is the primary agent, and because both independent and dependent agents are expressed by the single term "agent," there is a threefold division. Action (*karman*) is volitional effort (*ceṣṭā*). (18)
Thus, in the enumeration of qualities, according to the supreme Sāṅkhya treatise. || 19 ||

"Because of the existence [of Viṣṇu] in relation to the elements, the names, all living beings, and even the liberated ones; because of his being distinct from them, yet because of his being the omnipresent Viṣṇu;
and because of the identity of his own forms consisting of manifestations and so forth."
By means of the gradation of living beings, there is indeed mutual distinction.
And [the difference] between insentient things and sentient beings, between sentient beings and one another,
and between those and Viṣṇu, [is to be known] correctly, preceded by the knowledge of their respective characteristics.
Knowledge is declared to be of the nature of sattva, which is the direct cause of liberation. || 20 ||
Knowledge of the true nature of Viṣṇu or of another [deity] is said to be rājasa;
likewise, if one does not know Viṣṇu, or if one knows only mixed principles.
He who knows that the very living being called "the effect" is in fact the non-effect Brahman— because it is subject to transformation— is indeed one who knows everything.
Due to the knowledge of a single soul, he thinks, "I am all-knowing.
Lacking logical understanding and because his own position is irrational,
this person of limited vision considers that very irrationality to be a virtue.
The world speaks of what is not the true meaning because it is devoid of the knowledge of the true meaning.
Indeed, even by each one [of these] he becomes ignorant of the primary state, how much more so by all together?
"One who is endowed with all these [other] distinctions is the most preeminent among sinners," so it is said in the *Padma Purāṇa*.

The commentary on the phrase "knowledge of things as distinct" begins with "various states" (*nānābhāvān*) and so forth. Merely not perceiving the one, all-pervading Lord is *rājasa* (passionate). Knowledge of the One as being entirely manifold is *tāmasa* (dark). Furthermore, because the individual soul (*jīva*)—which is dependent on another and limited—is falsely conceived through forms such as liberation and the like as being full of qualities such as independence, the knowledge of its identity with the entire Brahman is *mahātāmasa* (greatly dark); how much more so, then, is the knowledge that "everything is merely that much"?

Furthermore, is there anything other than a single living soul even there? All knowledge that is causeless is characterized by *tamas*; how much more so that which possesses the aforementioned characteristics? That which is contrary to reality, being distinct from both existence and non-existence, is rightly considered *tāmasa* because it involves the conceptualization of objects otherwise; how much more so that which is endowed with the aforementioned specific qualifications? Generally, even limited knowledge is *tāmasa* due to its abundance of ignorance; how much more so that which is said to abound in false knowledge? Thus, there is no redundancy.

In one [system], the knowledge that the individual soul (*jīva*) is the full Brahman regarding the single effect of omniscience is illogical, based on an unreal conceptualization, and constitutes limited knowledge; or alternatively, these [views] are individually characterized as *tāmasa*. In the Māyāvāda, however, all of these [defects] are present together. Furthermore, in other systems as well, such things as "causelessness" and so forth are equally common among all those who propound contradictory doctrines. (21–22)

Because it has been stated, "Renouncing all actions in Me with a mind directed toward the Supreme Self," and because of the passages beginning with "Those who follow My teaching" and "But those who [do not]," this refers to that [teaching].

From the teaching regarding the sin incurred by the non-performance of the means to liberation, it is understood that the performance of all actions as an offering to the Lord, as well as the knowledge of that Viṣṇu as the supreme of all, are indeed mandatory. Because of the statement "with a mind directed toward the Self" (adhyātmacetasā), this includes the knowledge of the true nature of His essence and so forth. This is because, in the verse beginning with "But those who [perform] all actions," the state of having a mind directed toward the Self is explained by the words: "devoted to Me, meditating on Me through yoga that is indeed exclusive.
Thus, everything that is endowed with devotion to the Lord is purely sattvic. (23–25)
Precisely because of the certainty that everything is dependent upon the Blessed One, he is free from the assertion of "I" (anahaṃvādī).

"Indeed, he who has not performed what was excellent due to the power of devotion to the Blessed One—he, being a *prākṛta* (ordinary person), is a *dīrghasūtrī* (one who procrastinates), thinking, 'I shall do it later.
Thus it is stated in the *Śabdatattva*. The meaning of *dīrghasūtrī* is one who indicates the performance of a task whose time has arrived only after a long period of time.
One who is lazy, procrastinating, and endowed with [only] sattva is considered tāmasa;
one who is undisciplined, arrogant, vulgar, dishonest, and deceitful is rājasa.

"One who possesses each of these defects individually is declared *tāmasatāmasa*; the fruit of this is, respectively, the state of being a base man, the state of an animal, and [rebirth in] darkness. (28–30)

"And: 'That intellect by which one perceives some things as they truly are and others not as they truly are, is characterized by passion (rājasī); that which consists in false vision is indeed characterized by darkness (tāmasī). Thus [it is said]. (31–32)

And it is said: "The yoga of devotion belongs to Viṣṇu; that steadfastness (dhṛti) which is joined with it is characterized by goodness (sāttvikī). Thus, it is invariably restricted to the prescribed object [of worship]. (33-34)
The phrase "dreams and fear," and so forth, is an elliptical expression for everything that is prohibited.

As stated in the *Bhāgavata*: "Each of those [states] should be purely *sāttvika*; that which is *rājasa* is to be disregarded. Furthermore, the elders have spoken thus through such passages as "But the great-souled ones, O Pārtha, [take refuge in Me]" and "Fearlessness, purity of heart," and so on. (35–36)
"Through the grace of Viṣṇu and through the serenity of one's own mind, there arises sattvic happiness," so it is said in the Padma Purāṇa (37–39).
"Sattva" refers to all living beings. Because those who are liberated have transcended the *guṇas*, there is this distinction: "on earth, in heaven, and among the gods.
"Even though they move about as they please, the liberated do not belong to the earth and so forth;
for even while staying in a village, the virtuous are not vulgar, due to their extraordinary nature."
Among those, the lowest of men were tāmasa; the sattvika and rājasa types were there as well;
and the servants of the Daityas and the great Daityas themselves were the foremost among the tāmasa-tāmasa.
Among them, O Brahmins, men characterized by *rajas* are *rājasasāttvika*;
those established there in pure *sattva* are proclaimed as *parahaṃsas*.
The Haṃsa, Bahūdaka, Kuṭīcaka, Vanastha, Naiṣṭhika, and Gṛhī [are the six types of ascetics],
because passion increases progressively among them and external ritual action is predominant for each subsequent one.

The duties of the Paramahaṃsas consist solely of external practices such as tranquility and the like; for gods and others, there is an abundance of ritual action, yet there is never a total absence of the quality of passion (rajas).
For even when performing their duties, the minds of those [devotees] do not waver from Viṣṇu;
whereas, because others have fickle minds, their action is generally of a passionate (rājasa) nature.
If one knows that [the mantra] of Viṣṇu to be purely *sāttvika*, it serves as a reminder; however,
for the student (*brahmacārin*), there is the specific [practice] of sacrificing to the fire for the sake of dharma,
and likewise for the ascetic (*yatita*) there is the ancestral rite (*paitṛka*), and from that follows the taking of a wife by the householder (*gṛhin*).

"Non-attachment, renunciation of village life, and non-violence toward animals—this is the distinction of the forest-dweller from the householder; for all others, it is the same. And: "The Sāttvikas have very little rajas; the Kṣatriyas possess both sattva and rajas."
Vaiśyas and Śūdras are characterized by tamas due to a slight excess of sattva.
This distinction has been declared for those who belong to the social orders (varṇas) among the devotees of the Lord;
even a Pulkasa is superior in quality if he is always a devotee of the Lord.
Those who possess only the threefold knowledge (traividyamātra) and harbor doubts regarding the supreme excellence of Viṣṇu,
who do not acknowledge the superiority of any other over the Lord of Śrī, are the *rājasarājasa* [among the rājasa].

All those who are ignorant of Viṣṇu and devoid of hatred toward him— whether they be of the rājasa or tāmasa nature, or even those beginning with the ancestors (pitṛs) and gandharvas— are considered sages and deities.
Among those, the sattvic types are of three kinds, each subsequent one being superior to the preceding;
the deities are likewise of three kinds, beginning with Indra, Viriñca (Brahmā), and so forth.
"Śiva, Vāṇī, and Brahmā are each progressively higher;
[then] Sattvasattva, Mahāsattva, and Sūkṣmasattva, followed by Caturmukha. From that point until liberation is attained, such is the sequence of bliss within liberation. Thus it is said.

The meaning is that those who possess even a slight degree of affection for Viṣṇu among the *tāmasa* are the lowest of men, though they are *sāttvika*. Among the *sāttvika*, the *bhāgavata* brāhmaṇas and others are indeed *sāttvika*. Within the *sāttvika* residing in the *rājasa*, there is a classification by caste: the purely *sāttvika*, those *sāttvika* joined with a slight degree of *rajas*, those *sāttvika* joined with equal *rajas*, and those *sāttvika* joined with *tamas* slightly exceeding *sattva*. Because *sattva* is predominant, all of these, starting from these [lower grades] and proceeding upward, are fit for liberation, according to such statements as:
"From *sattva*, knowledge is born."

"And: 'One in whom sattva predominates is fit for liberation; likewise, one in whom [tamas] predominates is fit for the blinding darkness. One in whom tamas is further increased, or one in whom rajas abounds, or one who is equal [in the three guṇas], is a vessel for the path of transmigration. (40–41)
Tranquility, self-control, austerity, purity, forbearance, and uprightness,
as well as knowledge, realized wisdom, and faith in the Vedas— these are the duties of a Brahmin, born of his own nature.
These qualities are slightly inferior in a Kṣatriya compared to a Brāhmaṇa,
or they may even be superior to Brāhmaṇas in certain universal monarchs (cakravartins).
Indeed, kings such as Kārtavīrya and others are to be understood as ṛṣis. || 42 ||
"Valor, splendor, fortitude, skill, and not fleeing in battle;
generosity and lordliness—these, and other qualities as well, belong to the Kṣatriya. (43)
One who is a Kṣatriya but lacks the qualities of a Brahmin, or a Vaiśya who lives by agriculture and the like,
and one who is inferior even to them yet serves with tranquility and other virtues, is called a Śūdra.
"If a Śūdra possesses superior qualities, he is called a Brāhmaṇa or the like;
even a Brāhmaṇa with few qualities is proclaimed to be nothing but a Śūdra. A man who possesses divine qualities should be known as a god who has come among humans."

And thus: from the statement, "Having worshipped Him with one's own duty," it is understood that even among Kṣatriyas and others there is the persistence of tranquility (*śama*) and the other qualities. For without tranquility and the rest, worship performed with all one's being is not possible; indeed, "worshipping with all one's being" (*abhyarcana*) is worship performed thoroughly through tranquility and the like. Moreover, one does not attain perfection without tranquility and the rest, because it has been said: "The acts of sacrifice, charity, and austerity are not to be abandoned. And as the Blessed One said: "Tranquility is the steadiness of the intellect in Me; self-control is the restraint of the senses."

Furthermore, it is stated in various contexts regarding those respective duties that one must not be devoid of purity, austerity, tranquility, and so forth, even by such [means] as not being wounded; for Janaka, Taladhāra, and others were indeed endowed with all these qualities. Therefore, non-retreat in battle and sovereignty are the specific virtues of a Kṣatriya. These, along with agriculture and the like for the sake of livelihood, service for the sake of subsistence, officiating at sacrifices for the sake of livelihood, and the acceptance of gifts—these alone are the "other duties" (paradharma) of the remaining [classes].
"Valour, splendor, fortitude, dexterity, and generosity are preeminent in a Kṣatriya."
They are fewer in the Brāhmaṇa than that, and even fewer in the Vaiśya and the Śūdra than those.

Teaching and service for the sake of livelihood—excluding these for the virtuous—are to be understood as applying to the Brāhmaṇas and the others in their respective order, with the exception of teaching for the Śūdra. These are innate dispositions; however, other dispositions may also occur in some cases.
That which is contrary to one's nature, even if innate, must be abandoned by force;
whereas that which is auspicious, even if not natural, should be cultivated with diligent effort.
"However, sacrifices performed for the sake of sovereignty and other such [worldly] ends—even if auspicious—should not be undertaken by others [than the three higher castes].

Furthermore, it is required that Śūdras do not flee from battle for the sake of the Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas. And: "The seizure of wealth by force as well as corporal punishment [are the punishments for them]."
And teaching those who are not disciples likewise results in the destruction of the meaning.
This state of sovereignty should not be exercised by anyone other than a Kṣatriya;
all those who act contrary to the Dharma must always be restrained with effort by the Kṣatriyas.
Punishment for causing the loss of a limb or other parts [of the body] should be inflicted by Brahmins and others upon their disciples;
likewise, punishment may be applied even to the body of a disciple who has been entrusted to them by his own master or by himself.
Sons, younger brothers, and all others are by nature indeed disciples;
likewise, teachers, friends, companions, and fellow-students are also [disciples].
And all one's kinsmen, according to their respective capacities,
should be diligently instructed by wise men in those matters that ought to be learned.
In cases of insanity, there shall never be imprisonment or beating for a Guru.
Furthermore, others who commit sinful acts, as soon as they come within the range of vision of everyone,
must be restrained according to one's ability and in accordance with the place and time.
However, those who oppose what is supreme must be abandoned, even if they are one's gurus;
for even after instructing them to the best of one's ability over time, they do not become virtuous.
One who possesses supreme devotion to Viṣṇu must neither be abandoned nor punished;
yet, while a disciple may instruct his teachers, he must never instruct them as a teacher would.

"Householders are not to be instructed, even if they act in opposition, provided that they do not cause conflict with those superior to them. And so forth. "In times of distress, a Brahmin may practice the dharma of a Kshatriya or a Vaishya."
If the Kṣatriya fails, however, a Śūdra may not [act] for either a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya under any circumstances.
In times of distress, a Kṣatriya may follow the Brāhmaṇa dharma, and likewise in the distress of the Vaiśyas;
yet even when adopting the dharma of a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya must never be a receiver of alms.
In times of distress, a Vaiśya may follow the single dharma of a Śūdra and no other;
in his own times of distress, a Śūdra may follow the dharma of a Vaiśya, and in his own times of distress, he may follow that of a craftsman.
Even a Śūdra who follows the dharma of a Vaiśya shall never possess a syllable of the Veda;
nor shall even a Kṣatriya, except in extreme distress, do so without performing service for a quarter-part.
A Śūdra who performs the duties of a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya incurs no fault;
he should not be solicited for those tasks by his master, even when unasked.
Even acts pertaining to the Śūdra class may constitute one's own duty for a Kṣatriya in times of distress,
provided he possesses personal strength and that of his followers, O Lord.
For one who serves for the sake of dharma, service for the sake of wealth is inferior to that which is performed out of devotion to dharma and so forth;
yet, even more specifically, one who subsists by begging from a lord partakes in dharma.

"He who has superior strength in his arms is a Kṣatriya; he who is superior in knowledge is a Brāhmaṇa. These two are devotees of the Lord (Bhāgavatas), and with Him as their lord, these worlds belong to them. Thus it is stated in the Vyāsa-smṛti, verses 44–48.
The attainment of freedom from action (naiṣkarmyasiddhi), which is the attainment known as the destruction of all undesirable karma. || 49 ||

Listen now to how one, abiding in the manner about to be described, subsequently attains perfection through actionlessness (*naiṣkarmyasiddhi*) and reaches the presence of Mahālakṣmī, who is called Brahman. For it has been said: "My womb is the Great Brahman" and "I am indeed the foundation of Brahman"; and after stating "Having become Brahman, with a serene self," it will be said: "He attains supreme devotion to Me.
Thus, having abandoned the body through the destruction of all sins, he proceeds gradually toward the gods.
Having attained prosperity through His grace, when they once again flourished in devotion to Hari;
Furthermore, through that devotion, knowledge is attained once it has fully matured;
[this occurs] even regarding the body of Viṣṇu, who exists as one whose vision is direct, as was the case formerly.

"Even for one who has renounced the body and so forth, as long as they have not yet taken refuge in Viṣṇu, their virtues continue to increase; but having reached Keśava, those virtues remain steadfast. Thus it is said in the Mahāvarāha Purāṇa (50–52).

"Having become liberated, free from the sense of 'mine,' and tranquil," meaning that having attained the perfection of actionlessness (naiṣkarmyasiddhi), one becomes one with Brahman for the sake of further becoming. || 43-55 ||

Even while performing all prescribed duties, you should always do so by taking refuge in Me. For there is no intention here for you to act according to your own whims; were that the case, since the result would be the same even when prescribed duties are not performed, there would be a contradiction with the present context of such passages as "Remember Me and fight" and "Then [perform] your own duty. The word "even" (api), however, implies that not even a single action should be performed without taking refuge in Him. 56.

He states that there is a distinction between one who has taken refuge in the Blessed One and one who possesses the threefold knowledge (traividyā) solely by means of the mind: "all actions with the mind. He is "intent on Me" (matpara), meaning his state of being is such that He alone is supreme over all; therein also lies the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind. The "yoga of the intellect" (buddhiyoga) consists of withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra) and so forth. (57–58)

*Prakṛti* is the will of the Lord (*īśvarecchā*). For it is said: "O Infinite One, *prakṛti*, *vāsanā*, and likewise *icchā* (will) are declared by You. This [term *prakṛti*] is also applicable in such passages as "and by *prakṛti* alone [one performs] actions," for it is she who is primarily the impeller, having bound [beings] through nature, karma, and so forth. (51–60)
He states that very point: "The Lord of all beings," and so forth.

For it is said in the *Śabdanirṇaya*: "That is to be known as having an ascertained meaning where the Self alone is spoken of indirectly, just as in the passage beginning with 'That is Brahman' which is spoken by Viṣṇu. Furthermore, this is confirmed by the concluding statement, "Fixing your mind on Me" (61).
"The eternal abode is Vaikuṇṭha and so forth;
Śrī herself always dwells in the form of the world for Viṣṇu. Therefore, those Vaiṣṇavas in the world are indeed eternal, even though they are sentient beings."
Thus it is stated in the Āgneya Purāṇa: "Where neither rajas nor tamas, nor even sattva, exists," and so forth. (62–63)

The exposition of the essence of reality (*tattvasāra*) was concluded precisely in the verse beginning with "These two persons" (*dvāvimau puruṣau*). For the sake of praising that reality, the praise of the intellect [that perceives it] was likewise offered. Here, however, there is a conclusion regarding the essence of the means (*sādhanasāra*) in the words "the most secret of all" (*sarvaguhyatamam*). Since the passage beginning with "with Me as your mind" (*manmanāḥ*) has already been stated, the word "again" (*bhūyaḥ*) is used. In substance, even here, the superiority of Viṣṇu alone is declared. (64–65)

The statement "having abandoned all other dharmas" is a verbal expression of the same meaning as the phrase "all dharmas" used as a supplement to what was previously said. Furthermore, the instruction "take refuge in Me alone" is an explanatory conclusion to what was stated in "fixing the mind on Me" and so forth.
[This is defined as: "Always fixing the mind upon Him with the prior realization of His being the supreme of all, endowed with the greatest love for Him, and the surrendering of everything to Him."

The threefold worship is indivisible; by its very nature, it consists of the conviction "He protects me" and the remembrance "I am His. This is taking refuge in Viṣṇu, which bestows the fruit of liberation.

Thus it is stated in the Mahāviṣṇu Purāṇa. [This applies] to all sins committed throughout beginningless births; for here, since there is no possibility of attaining [any other state], the abandonment of sin is established by the principle of "how much more so" (*kaimutya*) upon the abandonment of dharma. || 66 ||

It should certainly not be spoken to one who lacks austerity (*atapaska*); the word *ca* (and) is used to indicate that there is an even greater fault in the case of one who does not desire to listen (*aśuśrūṣu*). Likewise, it should never be spoken to one who is not devoted (*abhakta*). The phrase "at any time" (*kadācana*) is understood [in the verse] to imply that it may sometimes be spoken even to one of little austerity or little desire to listen, provided there is an abundance of devotion. Furthermore, it should not be spoken to one who is not devoted and who is envious (*asūyu*); the word *ca* is used here as well. As stated in the *Śabdanirṇaya*: "The word *ca* is employed for conjunction, for excess, and for deficiency. And in the *Padma Purāṇa*: "One who is envious and sees only faults is more wicked than even one who is not devoted. (67)

From the statements, "He too is liberated" and "And not among humans [as such]," the great gradation (*tāratamya*) among the liberated is known. By the qualification "among humans," it is understood that even there, the gods possess superiority.
Liberation may occur through knowing Viṣṇu, but it is even greater than that through hearing the scripture (*śāstra*).
The bliss found in liberation is held to be even greater than that experienced by one reciting it.
"But for the commentator, there is equal happiness in liberation, and for no one else;
yet it is even greater for the gods, because he is the primary author of the commentary. Thus [ends the section] 68–72.
To avoid the objection, "Do as you wish," he follows the Blessed One by saying, "I shall do your bidding. (73–78)
Salutations to you, Vāsudeva, the most beloved among my loved ones,
who are replete with all virtues, the bestower of flawless bliss,
whose three divine forms have been fully proclaimed in the words of the Vedas.
Truly, that visible splendor of the Divine is thus established:
the first is the speech of Vāyu, the second is the body of nourishment (*pṛkṣas*), and the third is that which is honeyed; by means of this, the book has been composed for Keśava.
I bow to You, my beloved, who are free from every defect, possessed of all auspicious and excellent qualities, and worshipped by Bhūti, Svayambhū, Śarva, and the others.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavadgītā-tātparya-nirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda. || 18 ||
